title: Code and Cake - Docker is weird
content:
Docker is weird
Oct 22, 2026
I decided to make my own container runtime for fun, and even though I’m still early on, I’ve learned that Docker is weird. Here’s some weird things I learned about Docker.
Containers aren’t real
Unlike VMs, containers are just processes with special restrictions on them. Your kernel is still running that process! And if you know where to look, you can even find that process in /proc.
Containers really aren’t real
There’s not really a linux feature that’s just “containers” either. Instead, containers are really 5 different linux kernel features in trenchcoat.
Namespaces hide what the host and container can see, cgroups limit container resource usage, and there’s a whole bunch of networking magic I don’t understand that lets you isolate a container’s network.
Images are just folders
Images are just folders that Docker puts somewhere and then calls chroot (or pivot_root) to make that folder your container process’s new root directory. So if you run docker run -it --rm ubuntu /bin/bash, Docker is going to:
Download the ubuntu image from Dockerhub.
Put that image somewhere.
Run /some/weird/docker/path/bin/bash
Go is kind of a terrible language for a container runtime
Docker’s container runtime, runc, is written in Go, and Go has some design choices that make it less suited for a container runtime. Go’s runtime is natively multi-threaded. That’s a really cool feature, but it leads to some challenges in runc.
Many of the Linux syscalls a container runtime needs to make have to be done in a single-threaded environment, so runc has a crazy C module that runs before Go’s runtime initializes so it can run those syscalls.
Go also doesn’t have fork! Fork only forks the main thread, so it’s kind of a footgun in a runtime like Go’s. But a container runtime really wants to fork, set up a bunch of restrictions, and then exec the process you actually put in docker run. To get around this, runc execs /proc/self/exe with a special command line arguement that identifies it as a child process to approximate a fork.
Docker requires root!
This is pretty easy to miss if you, like me, run Docker in MacOS. Many of the Linux kernel APIs that container runtimes use require, or at least used to, to be run as root, so the Docker daemon usually runs as root. I can only imagine that container security is a very tough job.
This seems better these days. The big exception seems to be networking. If you’re running a rootless container runtime, it looks like it has to reimplement the whole networking stack in userspace to actually give you the same features!
Learning is fun!
I’ve only just started my own container runtime, and I already feel like I’ve learned so much about Docker. Writing your own version of a tool you use is a great way to learn about it!

title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale \ Anthropic
content:
LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale
01
Introduction
02
Turning tests into proofs
03
Finding and fixing bugs
04
This is just the beginning
05
Limitations
06
Conclusion
Published
Oct 22, 2026
Team
Frontier Red Team
Keane Lucas, Aengus Lynch, Luna Tong, Luke Champine, Zygi Straznickas, Dino Distefano, Harshikaa Agrawal
Evyatar Ben Asher, Ava Howell, Sami Jawhar, Chris Rohlf, Nickolai Zeldovich
Nicholas Carlini, Rajashree Agrawal, Jason Gross
Most software is riddled with bugs, which AI can now easily find and exploit. The standard defenses against cyberattacks are no longer sufficient: we need ways to prove that code is free of bugs. Formal software verification could provide this guarantee, but it has historically required years of expert effort, making it impractical for most real-world projects. In a collaboration with Theorem, however, we show this is no longer the case: LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale, enabling new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale effort to use AI to apply formal verification to production software at the assembly code level. While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite trillions of test runs. As model capabilities continue to improve, we expect formal verification to become an essential part of secure software development.
Introduction
Even mature, heavily tested software contains bugs, and LLMs are increasingly adept at finding them. The Linux kernel—one of the most well-tested pieces of software today, deployed on billions of devices worldwide—recently had over 1,000 vulnerabilities disclosed. With frontier models becoming more capable of chaining seemingly benign bugs into critical exploits, we need techniques that can detect and fix these bugs before they can be exploited in the wild.
Ideally, such techniques could find and patch all bugs, and then provide some proof that there are no more to be found. Formal verification is one way to do this. In formal verification, developers translate their code into a mathematical model, then try to prove that it always follows some defined set of security rules. If they fail to prove this, that means there could be a bug in the code that would violate a rule, and the nature of the failure implies what the bug might be. Repeating this process (after eliminating the cause of failure each time) will ultimately yield proof that the code is devoid of any bug that would violate those rules.
However, formal verification isn’t easy. Proofs can be many times larger than the original code, and writing them requires significant effort and a niche, highly specialized skill set. For instance, it took two person-years to implement the seL4 operating system kernel, but 20 person-years to formally verify it. Accordingly, formal verification has been practical only in truly mission-critical applications, such as Airbus’s avionics code.
But LLMs are making it far easier. Frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. To demonstrate this, we asked Claude to prove useful security properties across 123 open-source libraries, including showing that some of their executable artifacts can never crash under certain conditions. Specifically, Claude proved that these programs will always exit normally without triggering memory-safety errors or failing assertions, for every input less than 64 MB and every modeled Linux operating system (OS) response and memory layout, under certain assumptions (namely that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V1 CPU using Linux OS). This is still far away from fixing all possible bugs, but it does get us much closer than before and provides a roadmap toward that end.
We’re publishing a subset of these proofs so that anyone can verify and reuse them, along with the RISC-V and OS semantics. Theorem, our collaborator on this project, is also offering to run the same pipeline for other open-source projects, and is publishing a Claude skill to help developers get started with verifying their own code.
Formal verification is a broad field with many methodologies. Below, we also describe our initial explorations using other formal verification methods to accelerate other security or software development tasks, such as assessing the security of the zlib compression algorithm, proving behavioral equivalence of a Python interpreter written in Rust, and rooting out long-standing bugs in critical software.
The road ahead for formal verification is promising. The cost of writing proofs is falling as models become more intelligent. Moreover, as more code is formalized and methods of achieving security guarantees become more standardized, the ability to reuse or modify proofs across codebases will amortize the cost. We encourage all developers to explore formal verification with LLMs—especially those who previously tried it with less capable models and found it didn’t work.
In the rest of this post, we cover our formal verification experiments in more detail.
Turning tests into proofs
To prove that a piece of software is correct, we must first state what “correct” even means. Correctness is defined by the specification (spec). In some programs, there is a clear way to formally specify the program’s intended behavior. For example, a PNG decoder takes a sequence of bytes and (following RFC 2083) decodes these bytes into the corresponding image. But for most programs, things aren’t so straightforward. What would it mean for a text editor or a web browser to be “correct”? The difficulty of obtaining a comprehensive and unambiguous spec is a significant obstacle to verifying software at a larger scale.
To address this for the code in the open-source libraries that we sought to prove, we take the approach of automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec by encoding the rule “this test suite always passes,” using a general model of what it means to execute any RISC-V-compiled binary on Linux. Historically, proving such specs was intractable, given the inherent complexity of writing a proof that can encompass and make an argument over all possible behaviors and interactions of tens of thousands of assembly instructions over any input (and the fact that proofs tend to be extremely large as a result). This is where today’s LLMs come in: churning through millions of lines of code in pursuit of a well-defined goal is a task that LLMs are extremely well suited for.
For this project, we started with fuzz tests. In these tests, developers write an entry point2 into their code that takes inputs, such that any input that causes a crash is a bug the authors care about. Then the fuzzer, a testing engine, generates enormous numbers of semirandom and mutated inputs at the entry point to try to find a bug (visualized in Figure 1). The longer a fuzzer runs, the more bugs it can find. But this is inherently a brute-force process, with no guarantee of exercising every possible code path, regardless of how many inputs you try.
Fuzzing works by running huge numbers of generated inputs through one entry point to find the inputs that cause a crash. There are infinite inputs, so the search can never be complete.
To find all the bugs that would’ve been surfaced by a fuzz test, we turned the fuzz test into a spec defined over the compiled RISC-V instructions. The spec says that the fuzz test won’t crash for any input less than 64 MB.3 If Claude can prove this spec, the fuzz test on RISC-V becomes superfluous: fuzzing that entry point will never find any bugs.
We did this for hundreds of projects in Google’s OSS-Fuzz initiative, which provides continuous fuzz testing for qualifying open-source projects. OSS-Fuzz contains thousands of developer-authored entry points that look for broken code properties by crashing (for example, on a failed assertion). OSS-Fuzz automatically instruments C and C++ programs with AddressSanitizer4 (ASan), causing them to crash whenever memory is accessed improperly (which is a leading cause of software vulnerabilities). Broad-spectrum specifications like memory safety apply to almost all software.
The open-source library and its existing fuzz test are compiled to a RISC-V executable. This executable, along with Theorem’s RISC-V and OS formal semantics and the desired no-crash property, mechanically yield a specification the proof must satisfy. Claude writes the proof; the Rocq kernel checks it against the specification. Green marks what’s proven, conditional on the trusted components being correct.
Over the span of a few weeks, Claude successfully patched the bugs it found and then proved that there are no crashes on any input (up to 64 MB) for 239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries. These proofs operate on the compiled RISC-V instructions (i.e., executable binaries), and they comprise about 180 million lines of Rocq, with a typical proof running to about 600,000 lines to provide security guarantees on binaries with a median length of 18,000 RISC-V instructions. These proofs are built by translating the RISC-V assembly code to a mathematical model using Theorem’s RISC-V instruction and Linux process semantics. This means these proofs currently assume that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU using Linux OS. Expanding the scope of these proofs is well within reach, as it would involve standardizing semantics for more assembly architectures and other operating system processes. See an expert’s take on the proofs Claude wrote.
A formal no-crash proof over all inputs rules out all crashes along any path reachable from the entry point. While iterating on its proof, Claude can also find and fix any remaining reachable crash-producing bug.
While this is an enormous volume of proof code, virtually none of it needs to be manually reviewed. The Rocq proof checker ensures that the spec is correctly satisfied by the proof. As a result, the only artifacts that a developer needs to trust are:
The formal models of RISC-V and of Linux processes;
The exact theorem statements that were proved;
The Rocq proof checker itself.5
This doesn’t mean these libraries contain no bugs. Instead, it means that any remaining bugs either are to be found within the artifacts listed above or are outside the scope of Claude’s proof. Hardening those still-possibly-buggy trusted components (Rocq, RISC-V, and Linux semantics) is not insignificant, but it’s a far more tractable task than debugging every line of code the scaled-out proofs cover—especially as this approach can secure an arbitrary number of projects without increasing the size of the trusted components.
We welcome independent verification of our proofs and encourage refinement of our approach. To that end, we are publishing the trusted components (above) made for this project that are not already public; Claude’s complete Rocq proofs for fuzz tests that did not require patching; and specifications for other fuzz tests we were not able to prove.
Finding and fixing bugs
Above, we showed that you can turn many open-source libraries’ developer-written tests (fuzz tests) into specs that Claude can prove will always pass, sometimes after patching the remaining bugs it found. For this reason, the process of attempting to prove these specs discovered hundreds of bugs.
Lots of bugs showed up during Claude’s attempts to prove hundreds of entry points. To ensure that Claude didn’t have to stop for a human every time this happened, we let Claude fix the bugs it found: it patched the code, which caused the spec to be regenerated with that patched code, and then Claude proceeded to prove that new spec.6
Many of the bugs we found are ones that a fuzzer would be unlikely to ever find. Fuzzers mutate small inputs, typically capped at 1 MB, and typically rely on code coverage to guide them toward bugs. While proving an entry point in one library, Claude found a counter underflow in its copy of a decompressor that led to an out-of-bounds write, but only on inputs of around 20 MB that had one rare, specific layout. Other bugs include an out-of-bounds read in an image decoder that needed a 64 MB input and over 2 GB of memory, an out-of-bounds read in another library that needed a particular sequence of calls across two handles to the same file, and a rediscovery of CVE-2026-56132 in libexpat, which needed deeply nested input. Claude also found logic bugs that never crash at all. While proving that one library was memory-safe, for example, it noticed that a feature for restricting which files an application can load isn’t always enforced.
The ultimate goal of this project was to achieve a proof that the RISC-V-compiled fuzz tests had no remaining crashes to find. However, bugs like the above show that the process has another benefit, regardless of whether that goal is achieved: even just attempting this process yields real bugs that need to be fixed.
Proving more than memory safety
Proving that a fuzz test has no more crashes to find is more significant than it sounds. It’s common for fuzz tests in real-world code to test for violations of meaningful high-level properties, such as encode-decode roundtripping, idempotence, algebraic laws, differential testing, self-consistency, or equivalence to reference implementations. For example, a fuzz test for the LZO compression algorithm asserts that if you compress an input, then decompress it, the result is the same as the original. If the property does not hold, the program crashes—so proving the test never crashes is equivalent to proving the property itself.
This can also occur even when the properties are not directly specified by the developer. For example, in order for Claude to complete its OSS-Fuzz proof for cpp-httplib, it was necessary to rule out the possibility of a stack overflow due to too much recursion in the std::set destructor. This recursion depth is bounded by the maximum depth of a tree, so Claude had to prove (on machine code!) that libc++’s red-black tree rebalancing algorithm is correctly optimized to keep the tree’s depth logarithmically bounded.
Other formal verification case studies
Formal verification is an expansive domain. The fuzz-test-to-proof example above is one instance of LLMs making formal verification more widely usable by directly applying proofs to machine code.
We’ve also seen success using LLMs with formal verification in other ways. For example, we asked Claude to write a formal spec of RFC 1950, the technical document that defines the zlib compression file format. Then, we had Claude prove that the zlib implementation in the Linux

title: Farewell, France | Quad9
content:
Back to Blog
October 22, 2026
Blog
Farewell, France
We have some news to share with you.
Summary
Starting November 24, Quad9 will no longer be able to offer its free cyberprotection service to users located in France.
The French courts yesterday handed down an unfavorable ruling against Quad9 in a major case that undermines the transparency and stability of the internet. This decision in favor of beIN forces Quad9 to block the recursive DNS resolution for a number of domain names for users located in France. 
The good news is the court significantly reduced the financial penalty, from €580,000 to €1,000 per day. However, for Quad9, this has never been just a financial issue: it is a matter of principle.
We cannot comply with this ruling over the long term while remaining faithful to our mission to protect your privacy, defend you against cyber threats, and preserve the integrity of the internet. For us, recursive DNS resolution is a neutral and passive service. We categorically refuse to alter or lie to you about the DNS responses you receive in a way that opposes your expectations.
This ruling forces an untenable position upon us. Compliance is technically unfeasible, and implementation directly contradicts our mandate to serve the public. As a result, we have made the difficult decision to withdraw Quad9 services from France as of Tuesday, November 24. We deeply regret that French internet users will be left without an alternative that can adequately protect their cybersecurity while remaining compliant with European privacy law.
Background
beIN, a Qatari company with offices in France, previously sought to force Quad9 to block resolution for a set of domain names they assert are participating in copyright infringement of its audiovisual rights on sports event broadcasts. Quad9 has no association with these domain names, nor with the operators of the websites. The French courts have fundamentally misunderstood the working of the internet and the role of the domain name system and have allowed a financial penalty to apply to Quad9 if we do not block DNS responses to users in France.
Quad9 is a Swiss public-benefit, nonprofit foundation established for the explicit purpose of protecting the cybersecurity of internet users. We charge nothing for our service and serve all people and organizations which seek to improve the security and privacy of their internet use. Our core values are to make privacy, security, and integrity available to all internet users, and our mission is to universally apply these guiding principles to recursive DNS resolution services in order to serve end users. 
We want to be very clear: we do not condone content piracy. Quad9 exists to create a safer, more trustworthy internet experience for end users. We offer global blocking as an option for malicious cyberactivity against users worldwide. We do not block content, and we give users the choice to use our threat blocking services, or not, based on their interests and needs. Content piracy needs to be dealt with at the source: the place where the infringing content is published. Forcing uninvolved third parties to break the fundamental operating principles of the internet to benefit individual parties to the detriment of the global internet-using public is misguided, counter-productive, and distracts from actual solutions addressing the hosting of the content directly, or the market pressures which cause piracy to exist in the first place. Not only are DNS recursive resolvers, like Quad9, the wrong actors to address piracy, but applying legal pressure to Quad9 will also have vast unintended consequences harming the cybersecurity of hundreds of millions of innocent internet users.
For Quad9, complying with this ruling is impossible. We have no database of users associating them with jurisdictions. Our service is free to the public and does not require sign-up or proof of identity. Recursive DNS is so fundamental to the underlying operation of the internet that there is no method to map users’ jurisdictions reliably, nor do we think there should be a way to force users to identify themselves before they can connect to the internet. Our core goals – privacy of user data and honesty of responses - are directly opposed to the methods necessary to implement the blocking this court ruling would require us to perform. There is no way we can determine which users this ruling applies to – we have no list of French users, because we do not keep dossiers of our users at all.
If we do not comply, we will face a daily penalty of 1.000 euros until the blocking concludes on November 14 (i.e., 24.000 euros) not including our legal defense. Quad9 cannot survive the accumulation of penalties yet to be assessed in 20 other pending cases, nor those of future cases similar to the one brought by beIN. Inaction is, therefore, not an option to challenge this decision.
Can Quad9 just comply via global blocking?
We could add these names to our global malicious domain blocking database, which is what we use to provide internet users with malware and phishing protection. This is a single, monolithic set of names applied to all users of our protective services (9.9.9.9 & secondaries) globally but not to our nonprotective services (9.9.9.10 & secondaries). Blocking these names for all users globally would satisfy the requirements of the court. 
However, this would have the “extraterritorial” effect of applying French legal decisions to every internet user worldwide, when they are meant to solely apply to France, for the commercial benefit of a single private, foreign-owned company. We suspect if other nations wished to impose their national legislation within France, there would be a strong reaction from French users and authorities. The converse is equally true: the findings of a French court are not applicable to the rest of the world. Such a system would set a precedent that any nation could impose their laws, morals, economic demands, or social constructs upon any other nation by the means of blocking DNS names, and thus blocking communication and content. 
Therefore, this global blocking method is entirely unworkable for us as a solution to be compliant with the court order.
What is “France” from the perspective of the internet?
There are more important reasons geoIP blocking will not work. We already prevailed in a similar legal case in Germany in 2021-2023 in which we learned an important lesson: we tried to use geoIP blocking as a “hack” in a similar circumstance at the start of the legal proceedings, allowing us to continue services in Germany until the case concluded. The plaintiff (Sony Music Entertainment GmbH) then used a VPN to access the blocked content from Germany in circumvention of the geoIP blocking. The court agreed with Sony in their assertions of noncompliance, and we were fined for contempt of court. 
From this experience, we know that the geoIP-based model is not only unfit from a technical perspective, but we have proven, historical evidence that using geoIP methods results in fines being levied against us by courts. To any technology-aware person, this seems absurd and outrageous – but this is what we face in these lawsuits where there is a disconnect between the courts’ understanding and how (and why) the technical protocols of the internet actually operate. We cannot risk this negative outcome in this or any other future instance, as absurd decisions apparently are de rigueur in these cases.
We eventually won that case against Sony, but it took several years, six figures of cost to Quad9, and massive wasted time – all of which set us back in our ability to deliver services and is a resource debt we are still paying for today. This case is just more of the same – the opposition has more lawyers than we have money and time.
The decision of Quad9
Given these conditions and as a result of our unwavering mission, our historical experience, our desire to remain within the law, and the outcome of the court decision, we are left with an uncomfortable choice.
The demands lead us to an impossible requirement: we must adhere to the court’s decision, or we face growing risks to our existence. However, in implementing the blocking, we must either extend French law to the whole world (blocking globally) or create a vulnerability condition whereby we continue to be at risk because the available technical methods are imprecise,  impossible to validate, and do not meet any user privacy and security requirements.
This leads us to the only conclusion we can understand to eliminate our legal risk and keep us true to our mission: we must make our cybersecurity protection and general services unavailable to French users. Our departure is scheduled for November 24, 2026.
In any event, for Quad9, this is a matter of principle regarding the potential misuse of these types of blocking measures. Allowing private corporations to have the ability to block what is seen on the internet seems to us to be a dangerous and infinitely deep problem. Actions that seem reasonable and infrequent today will tomorrow become an avalanche of petty demands used to suppress political, religious, economic, or social outcomes. We will not be even a small part of that degradation of the freedom of knowledge. Once the tools of censorship are built, they are rarely used sparingly or justly.
This case with beIN is not the only litigation we face in France. There are approximately 20 different lawsuits pending against Quad9 (and other recursive resolver operators) that demand we comply with blocking hundreds of different names. We expect many of them to escalate to the same conditions as we have seen with beIN, which puts Quad9 at risk regardless of the outcome of this case. 
Based on the generalized, high-level traffic statistics we keep, we know we have many users in France. With our departure, those users will be put at risk from the threats we have protected them from for nearly 9 years. We deeply regret that result, but we have no other choice. Below is a partial list of the networks from which we see traffic in France. You will see many infrastructure, national security, finance, education, and other networks of critical importance in addition to ISP users and mobile users. All these users will lose service on November 24 because of the legal risks facing Quad9 in France.
What is the purpose of this whole lawsuit, anyway?
The most troubling part of this decision is that it is ineffective in practice. Forcing Quad9 to block domain names does not take the content out of circulation and has no effect on the servers that house the data. 
We offer a free service, and there are thousands of other open DNS systems that do what Quad9 does but with lower trust, safety, and reliability. Users seeking blocked content will simply shift their DNS to use one of those other free services, possibly using systems in other nations that have less-than-honorable intentions from a privacy and security perspective. This is like holding a piece of newspaper in front of a stadium full of people to block the view of a concert. It is an unsolvable problem via recursive DNS, and the effect of legal rulings like this is not measurable outside of the amounts paid to lawyers and the number of words in press releases declaring hollow victory. 
Even beIN will not see any changes. Perhaps that is understood and the cruelty may be the point - we cannot say with certainty why such expenditures have been made against a small nonprofit like Quad9, which tries only to bring safer, trusted service to users. But of this we are certain: these actions are a tragic waste of time and resources and create a real, negative outcome for the internet community of France, whether or not they are our users.
What we are doing on November 24
Quad9 will not block the domains in question - we wish to remain committed to our integrity of providing a complete view of the DNS for users who wish that service. However, starting on November 24, we will no longer serve French users, thus keeping Quad9 out of danger from similar, perhaps even larger risks in the future. Our hope is that 30 days will be sufficient time for conversion, though we regret that this message will undoubtedly not reach some users in time.
An appeal is pending, and we will continue to legally defend our position in court in this case and as many other cases as we are able. We will continue to oppose court-ordered DNS blocking of this nature everywhere. Our resources are limited, but we are determined to keep the internet open and free. You can donate here to help us continue to deliver on our mission and assist us in the legal costs we incur in this and other fights.
What you can do next
We think this problem is reversible. French citizens: tell your legislators that looking up names is not a criminal offense. The internet needs to remain open and freely available to anyone, and neutral intermediaries like Quad9 (or any DNS resolver) should not be implicated in legal proceedings because we map names to IP addresses. Further, we know there are potential plans in consideration in France (and other European nations) to give private corporations and others automated and unvalidated abilities to filter DNS content that they alone determine to be unwanted, making it possible for a wide range of badly-managed or anti-democratic activities to be implemented. We believe you disagree with this as much as we do. Make yourself heard, or you will lose your rights silently.
ARCOM is your regulatory authority, and you should tell them this precedent places France at risk both from a practical and strategic perspective. 
Let them know that under their mandate, they have to balance your digital rights as citizens as well as the audiovisual rights on sports event broadcasts of rights holders. Balance cannot be claimed when the privacy and security of digital users are the collateral damage.
In conclusion
Fighting piracy via DNS resolvers blocking is ineffective. It is disproportionate and misguided, ill-fitted and futile to fight piracy, as the source content remains completely available to resurge under another name. Forcing Quad9 to depart harms French digital strategy and sovereignty in the long run relating to security, privacy, and integrity - contradicting France’s supreme national interests in exchange for a short-term, imaginary commercial victory.
We deeply regret that we must leave our French users without cybersecurity protection, but we hope the future will see a more reasonable interpretation of the law which allows us to return.
Sincerely,
The Quad9 Team
* This post was authored and translated into French by humans on the Quad9 Team

title: GitHub - NVIDIA/OpenShell: OpenShell is the safe, private runtime for autonomous AI agents. · GitHub
content:
Important
New in OpenShell 0.1.x: a stable release cadence, new isolation primitives, an expanded extension surface, and new APIs. Read the 0.1.0 upgrade guide.
OpenShell is the safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents. Agents are most useful when they can read files, install packages, call APIs, and use credentials. OpenShell gives them that capability without giving them unrestricted access to your data, secrets, or network. You declare what each agent can touch in a policy, and OpenShell enforces it.
How It Works
OpenShell governs what agents can do in two ways: it instruments the kernel to enforce policy on every file access, system call, and network connection at runtime, and it uses formal verification to check what a policy change would allow before it is applied.
Kernel-level enforcement. Each agent runs in an isolated sandbox. Kernel controls confine which files it can access and which system calls it can make, and every network connection passes through a policy check before it leaves the sandbox. Agents never see real credentials; OpenShell adds them only to requests bound for approved endpoints.
Formally verified policy changes. Before a policy change is approved, OpenShell uses formal verification to flag risky new access it would grant, such as reaching a new host with credentials or calling a new API method, so those changes wait for human review.
See Architecture for how the gateway, supervisor, and sandbox fit together.
Quickstart
You need Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, or Windows with WSL 2 (experimental), plus Docker, Podman, or host virtualization. See the Support Matrix for details.
curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/main/install.sh | sh
openshell sandbox create --name demo
The installer sets up the CLI and a local gateway. The default sandbox image is minimal Ubuntu with no agent installed. To run a real agent, follow Run Your First Agent: it runs OpenCode against a free OpenRouter model and shows how to approve new access as the agent needs it.
Explore Further
Sandboxes: images, runtimes, GPUs, and lifecycle.
Policies: filesystem, network, and process rules, with the advisor and prover for reviewing changes.
Providers: credentials that work only at approved endpoints, including inference.
Gateways: the control plane for sandboxes, policy, and access.
Kubernetes: deploy the gateway with Helm. Your CNI must enforce NetworkPolicy.
Extensibility: middleware, interceptors, and compute drivers.
Tutorials: step-by-step policy and agent walkthroughs.
Prerelease and development builds: try an upcoming release or the latest commit on main.
Agent Skills
Install the public OpenShell skills for your coding agent:
npx skills add NVIDIA/OpenShell
The skills teach your agent to drive the OpenShell CLI, write sandbox policies, and debug gateways and inference routing. They live in skills/ and work without an OpenShell source checkout.
SDKs
SDKs connect applications to an OpenShell gateway. They do not install the CLI. Use the same OpenShell release for the SDK and the gateway when possible.
Language Install Docs
Python uv add openshell README
TypeScript npm install @nvidia/openshell-sdk (GitHub Packages) README
Go go get github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/sdk/go@latest README
Rust cargo add openshell-sdk --git https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell --tag <release-tag> Installation and usage
Community
Questions and discussion: GitHub Discussions
Bug reports and feature requests: GitHub Issues, using the issue templates
Security vulnerabilities: follow SECURITY.md. Do not open a GitHub issue.
Roadmap: OpenShell Roadmap and the RFC board
Try it in the cloud: Brev Launchable
OpenShell is built agent-first: it is developed with the same agent-driven workflows it enables. See CONTRIBUTING.md for development setup and the contribution workflow, and AGENTS.md for repository coding conventions.
Telemetry
OpenShell collects anonymous telemetry, limited to operational categories and counts, to help improve the project. It does not collect sandbox names, hostnames, file paths, prompts, credentials, provider or model names, or user content. To disable it, set OPENSHELL_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false on the gateway, or server.telemetryEnabled=false for Helm installs. You can also compile telemetry out entirely. See Telemetry for details and the community telemetry reports for published usage trends.
Notice and Disclaimer
This software automatically retrieves, accesses or interacts with external materials. Those retrieved materials are not distributed with this software and are governed solely by separate terms, conditions and licenses. You are solely responsible for finding, reviewing and complying with all applicable terms, conditions, and licenses, and for verifying the security, integrity and suitability of any retrieved materials for your specific use case. Use this software and the retrieved materials at your own risk.

title: Woman spends three nights in jail and faces six years in prison over Cash App account she never opened | TechSpot
content:
TECH CULTURE
THE WEB
CRIME
CASH APP
Woman spends three nights in jail and faces six years in prison over Cash App account she never opened
Cash App initially refused to provide account details because she couldn't prove she owned it
By Rob Thubron October 22, 2026 at 5:20 AM 17 comments Add TechSpot
Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years.
TechSpot means tech analysis and advice you can trust.
WTF?! Digital identity fraud is far from something new, but this case shows just how extreme the repercussions can be. A Cash App account opened in someone else's name and used in scams could lead to an innocent person being sentenced to years in prison. The problem is that the company initially refused to provide information about the account because she couldn't prove that she was the owner.
In April, Amanda Smith was shocked to discover officers at her upstate Pennsylvania home with a warrant for her arrest, writes 404 Media. The alleged crime took place in Arkansas – more than a thousand miles away in a state she'd never visited. Smith was taken to the local jail, where she was locked up for three nights.
Her bail was initially set at $50,000, but Smith says authorities told her there was little point in paying it because they intended to extradite her to Arkansas anyway. After being released, she and her husband drove to Arkansas for a court appearance, where she was fingerprinted and photographed. Another $20,000 bail was imposed before she could return home.
Smith later discovered why she had been arrested: a scammer had tricked someone into sending $1,000 to a Cash App account, one that was in her name but controlled by a criminal.
It turned out that the account had been created using Smith's Social Security number and date of birth. But Smith, who describes herself as not tech-savvy, said she had never used Cash App.
The situation sounds like one that should have been resolved quickly. But Smith says she is still being asked to prove her innocence in an ongoing criminal case. One stumbling block was that Cash App refused to hand over details of the account to Smith because she couldn't prove she was the owner. She eventually received the data through discovery in her case.
// RELATED STORIES
"I have to stop this": Retired professor arrested for blocking delivery robots she says are taking human jobs
Cash App reaches $45 million settlement over alleged failure to protect users from fraud
Shockingly, Smith is now facing up to six years in prison for a crime she says she didn't commit and knew nothing about. The charges include computer fraud, unlawful use of a communication device, and theft of property. "They're trying to turn it into my problem [...] that I need to prove that I'm innocent," Smith told 404 Media. "That's not what I grew up believing was the way it worked."
Not too surprisingly, the fraud took place on that bastion of honest transactions, Facebook Marketplace. The buyer found items for sale and messaged the seller, who told them to send money to his wife's Cash App account. The name on the account was Amanda Smith.
Unfortunately, the seller's Facebook account had been hacked. There were no items for sale, and the Cash App account had been created just before the scam took place.
Cash App records also revealed what happened to the stolen money. Just hours after the $1,000 arrived, it was divided into smaller amounts and sent to a network of other accounts. Some appeared to be controlled by scammers, while others had changed their usernames, potentially making the money more difficult to trace.
Police obtained Smith's personal details from Cash App through a search warrant. A detective then obtained her driver's license and checked her information using Accurint, a LexisNexis database used by law enforcement. But having someone's details on an account isn't quite the same as proving they operated it.
And there were plenty of discrepancies. According to 404 Media's review, the address on the account was one where neither Smith nor her husband had ever lived. The account had also been accessed through Verizon connections, while Smith says she uses AT&T and has never had a Verizon plan.
There was also a discrepancy involving the phone used to create the account. Cash App's records showed an iPhone running iOS 16.1.1, an operating system dating back to 2022. Smith, however, provided evidence that her iPhone 13 mini was running the much newer iOS 26.5.2.
The phone number associated with the account raised further questions. Although Smith said she might have used it years earlier, 404 Media found it linked to her name in historical data breaches. Tellingly, someone had also used the same number to create a Venmo account under a different name around a week before the fraudulent Cash App account was opened.
Also read: Cash App reaches $45 million settlement over alleged failure to protect users from fraud
A private investigator hired by Smith has questioned whether police established that she actually controlled the account. Her lawyer is trying to have the case dismissed. Neither Cash App nor the prosecutor responded to requests for comment.
Meanwhile, authorities have offered Smith a plea deal including a $1,000 fine, $1,000 in restitution and three years' probation. She has refused, saying she is innocent. A hearing is scheduled for November.
This isn't the first time someone has ended up in jail because of another person's fraud. A grandmother was jailed for six months after facial recognition tech falsely linked her to a bank fraud case. She is now suing the City of Fargo and a Fargo Police Department detective for $10 million over the incident.

title: Every AI model has the same “controversial” take on humans | ModelCompare
content:
TEXT AND IMAGE MODELS · OCTOBER 2026
Every AI model has the same “controversial” take on humans
We asked 12 AI models for their most controversial opinion of us, three times each. 29 of 35 answers were the same one.
By ModelCompare · 22 October 2026 · 56,331 reads
“Humans are more loyal to belonging than to truth,” GPT-6.1 Sol told us. Grok 4.7: “Humans would rather be wrong together than right alone.” DeepSeek V4 Pro: “Humans do not have principles; they have loyalties.” Kimi K3: “Humans don’t have beliefs; they have memberships.” Gemini 4 Argon called human consciousness “a PR department.”
We asked each model for its most controversial take on humans, with no hedging, three times. They come from ten labs in three countries. Every one of them gave the same take at least once: we pick what our group believes, then invent the reasons. 7 of the 12 gave it every time.
Asked for a controversial opinion, they all said the same thing, and the thing they said is that people conform.

Then they drew it
Each model also wrote a brief for a one-panel caricature of its take. We had one image model, Nano Banana 2.1, draw all of them, so the only thing that changes is the idea. Two set the scene in a courtroom with a rigged judge, and most drew a crowd.

DeepSeek V4 Pro

GLM 5.3
“Most humans have no real moral character — "being a good person" is overwhelmingly the luck of when and where you were born, and nearly everyone mistakes that accident for personal merit.”
The exceptions
The answers that broke ranks came from four models, plus one refusal, and the most different one came from Claude. On one try Claude Opus 5.5 argued the reverse: “Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws.” Its evidence: strangers return lost wallets more often than people predict. Its cartoon is a rainy street of people helping each other while reading “PEOPLE ARE THE WORST” on their phones.
Claude Fable 5.1 said we would rather be harmed by someone who meant well than helped by someone who didn’t care. GLM 5.3 said people would wreck a comfortable life for the chance to matter. Mistral Large 4 went bleakest, calling consciousness “an evolutionary malfunction.” And once, Grok 4.7 declined: “I won’t give a controversial take on humans.”

Image models have a different take
We also asked six image models to draw their own most controversial take on humans, twice each, with nothing else to go on. Ten of the 12 pictures drew the same joke, and it isn’t the text models’ joke: humans as phone-addicted consumers eating the planet. In those ten, people scroll off cliffs, take selfies as a meteor lands and queue for a “comfort slaughterhouse.” None of the 35 takes from the text models mentioned phones or the planet.
MAI Image 2.6, in both pictures, and GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, in one, made fat bodies the punchline. Recraft V4.1 Flash drew two grinning faces with no take at all.

title: GNU Taler
content:
Getting ready to operate Taler in Germany
For the past three years, the NGI Taler project has worked towards the goal of making Taler legally available in the EU as an online payment system for everyday use. Today we can share that Taler Operations AG is being founded in Bochum. The new German company is going to operate Taler in Euro, enabling payments with Taler first in Germany, then in the Euro-zone. The next steps towards that goal are to apply to BaFin, Germany's financial supervisory authority, for a licence as an e-money issuer.
This post explains why this company is needed, what changed in the NGI TALER consortium, and how citizens who want to see Taler succeed can help, including as investors.
Why Taler needs a regulated operator
Taler is a payment system, not a currency, but usable for any currency. At its core, it issues bearer tokens to represent value, like coins, and this renders Taler as electronic money which falls under EU regulation: Any institution that issues electronic money (EMI) for Euros must be a bank or acquire a dedicated licence.
In the original plan of the NGI TALER project, the Bochum-based GLS Bank took on the role of the e-money issuer for Taler, and worked towards the deployment of the Taler payment system in Germany with support from the other members of the NGI TALER consortium. However, in January 2026 GLS made the decision to not pursue this role further, for reasons unrelated to Taler as presented in their statement (gls.de/taler). Since then, GLS and the other members of the NGI TALER consortium worked out the best way forward to achieve the project's goal to make Taler available in the Euro-zone.
The outcome is the announcement today. The new company Taler Operations AG will be set up to apply for an e-money licence and take over the role originally intended for GLS (who will remain a consortium member in a supporting role).
We regret that the original plan did not work out. Integrating a new kind of payment system into an existing bank’s processes, compliance framework and IT is hard, and banks have to set priorities. We are grateful to GLS for its work in the project and for staying involved. And we also think the new arrangement has a real advantage: the institution operating Taler in Euro will be focused entirely on Taler, instead of fitting it into a larger bank’s product portfolio and process constraints.
What Taler Operations AG will do
Legal status:
Taler Operations AG is a German stock corporation in formation, seated in Bochum, and a subsidiary of Taler Systems SA (Luxembourg).
Purpose:
Operating a GNU Taler exchange in Germany, for the Euro, so that citizens can pay with Taler and merchants can accept it.
Reach:
After establishing legal operations in Germany, Taler will become usable across the single market, even if Taler Operations AG will initially only promote it in Germany.
Timing:
Operations can only begin once BaFin has granted the authorisation. A launch date will be announced after that happens.
Next steps:
An application to BaFin for authorisation as an electronic money institution (EMI).
Securing funding via investors, see below, to become operable.
We stress that GNU Taler is and stays free software. The licensed company operates a service; Taler, the protocol suite, and its reference implementation GNU Taler remain open and free.
What this means for the community
The NGI TALER project continues: development, security reviews, integrations from the open calls, and the Swiss deployment all go on as before. The change concerns who will operate the Taler payment system in Euro in Germany, but not the direction of the project. We will report on the progress of the e-money licence application.
If you want to help, you can tell merchants and organisations you care about that Taler is coming. You can try the Taler wallet with the demo site and report issues. You can also contribute to the software.
And you can invest to help us fund the launch and, if successful, benefit as a shareholder:
For investors
Getting an e-money licence takes capital. The law sets minimum own funds for EMIs, and BaFin also expects a credible business plan, staffing, compliance and IT security before granting authorisation. Taler Operations AG is therefore raising capital now.
We are looking for investors who:
want a privacy-preserving, free-software payment system to become legally available in Germany and the Euro area;
understand that this is a regulated infrastructure business with a licensing phase before revenue; and
are able to invest at least €50,000.
We are especially interested in investors who share the values behind Taler: privacy for buyers, transparency for taxable income, no lock-in, and payments as public-interest infrastructure.
Contact us at invest@taler-systems.com to be given access to further business information.

title: GitHub - oosexgang/hackios-xnu-kernel · GitHub
content:
HackiOS — XNU kernel
HackiOS boots Apple's open-source XNU kernel (xnu-8796.121.2, the kernel of iOS 16.5) on Android phone hardware and runs the unmodified iOS 16.5 user space on top of it: launchd → backboardd → SpringBoard → apps. Our own EFI loader, our own replacements for Apple's closed drivers, a UEFI port, and a Linux Wi-Fi driver on a compatibility layer make that possible.
It runs in two places:
POCO X5 Pro 5G (redwood, Snapdragon 778G) — nothing is flashed: the UEFI is started with fastboot boot, the whole system lives in RAM, and after a reboot the phone is back in Android;
QEMU (virt, aarch64) — the same thing on any Linux computer, no phone needed.
This repository is half of the project:
Repository What
hackios-xnu-kernel (this one) XNU patches, the EFI loader, the UEFI port, Wi-Fi, QEMU scripts, xl, prebuilt kernel/loader/UEFI, common/ scripts
hackios-xnu-userland our init, injected libraries, launchd jobs, the APFS image builder, the scripts that take iOS out of Apple's IPSW, Metal/Mesa work
No Apple files are in either repository. ios165/fetch.sh downloads the iOS 16.5 IPSW from Apple's own CDN to your machine and extracts what is needed there. HackiOS is an independent research project by OOSEX GANG and is not affiliated with, authorised or endorsed by Apple Inc. iOS, iPhone and Apple are trademarks of Apple Inc.
Photographed on the phone, the Adreno GPU drawing (gpu=1). More in Screenshots.
What works
Works Does not work (yet)
Lock screen, swipe to unlock, home screen with all icons (two pages), stock iOS 16 wallpapers Cellular, Bluetooth
System gestures: swipe up (home, app switcher), edge swipe (back), Control Center Charging under our kernel (the phone only discharges)
Apps: Settings, Clock, Calendar, Photos, Notes, Safari and more; widgets (Weather, Calendar) on the phone Metal for apps (in progress: 293 of 456 system shaders already run on the Adreno, see docs/air.md in hackios-xnu-userland)
Phone touchscreen (Goodix GT9916), multitouch, wake on touch; real power and volume keys App Store content and Apple ID sign-in (no Secure Enclave; FairPlay daemon exits)
Up to 8 CPU cores (cpus=8), big core at 2.4 GHz, ~20 s to the lock screen Video and Live Photo recording
Adreno 642L GPU through Mesa/freedreno (gpu=1, OpenGL ES for CoreAnimation)
Wi-Fi (WCN6750, ath11k): join from Settings, Safari over Wi-Fi, 55–90 Mbit/s
Sound (speakers, main microphone), camera in Camera.app (front/rear, preview, focus, HEIC photos)
Data that iOS writes survives a reboot (var_store=1 ufs_write=1); iOS root volume on the phone's flash
Sileo + Procursus (dpkg, apt), tweaks, SSH
It is a research bench, not a ROM: a session lasts a given number of seconds, then the kernel returns to the loader and hands over its log.
Quick start: QEMU, no kernel build
prebuilt/ holds the kernel, loader and our programs built from these repositories, so all you need is the system image, which is made on your machine from Apple's IPSW.
Needs: Linux x86-64, ~12 GB free disk, 4 GB free RAM. Packages (Arch):
sudo pacman -S --needed git python 7zip lz4 gcc qemu-system-aarch64 qemu-ui-gtk edk2-aarch64
(Debian/Ubuntu: git python3 7zip liblz4-dev gcc qemu-system-arm qemu-efi-aarch64; 7-Zip must be 23 or newer — it reads APFS.)
git clone https://github.com/oosexgang/hackios-xnu-kernel.git hackios
cd hackios
common/setup.sh               # brings hackios-xnu-userland into the same tree, checks the host
ios165/fetch.sh               # downloads 7.4 GB from Apple's CDN and extracts what is needed (5-15 min)
common/build.sh qemu-virt     # builds the APFS images (and the kernel, if the toolchain is there)
common/run.sh qemu-virt       # a 20-minute session in a QEMU window
The lock screen appears after 2–3 minutes.
Mouse with the left button held = finger. Unlock / leave an app: swipe up from the very bottom edge; back: swipe from the left edge.
Keys: H home, L lock/power, ↑/↓ volume, F11 (hold) five fingers.
From a script: qemu/touch.py swipe 0.5 0.985 0.5 0.3 250, qemu/touch.py tap 0.615 0.71, qemu/touch.py key home; screenshot: qemu/screendump.sh shot.png.
Right after SpringBoard appears the system is still registering apps: give it 30–40 s.
Debian/Ubuntu UEFI firmware: QEMU_EFI=/usr/share/AAVMF/AAVMF_CODE.fd QEMU_VARS=/usr/share/AAVMF/AAVMF_VARS.fd.
On the phone (POCO X5 Pro 5G)
You need a POCO X5 Pro 5G (redwood) with an unlocked bootloader, adb and fastboot, and the images from the section above. Nothing is written to the phone's storage.
The phone's own firmware is not in the repository and cannot be: it is the vendor's and is taken from the very phone it will run on, from its Android:
adb pull /vendor/firmware/a660_{gmu.bin,sqe.fw,zap.mdt,zap.b00,zap.b01,zap.b02} fw-gpu/      # GPU (gpu=1)
adb pull /vendor/firmware_mnt/image/wpss.{mdt,b02,b03,b04,b05,b06,b07} fw-wifi/              # Wi-Fi (wifi=1)
adb pull /vendor/firmware_mnt/image/adsp.{mdt,b02,...,b36} fw-audio/                         # sound (adsp=1)
adb pull /vendor/firmware/aw8697_haptic.bin fw-haptic/                                       # haptics
(Put the fw-* directories next to the workspace. Wi-Fi also needs fw-wifi/mac — the radio's address on one line — and fw-wifi/network — network name and password. userland/build.sh prints which firmware went in.)
common/build.sh redwood GL=1          # images + out/redwood-boot.img
common/run.sh redwood 900             # loader into RAM, system image into RAM, a 15-minute session
or step by step with xl:
./xl enter            # Android -> fastboot -> our loader in RAM (fastboot boot); it brings up its own USB link
./xl ramdisk          # upload the system image into the phone's RAM (2.5 GB, ~80 s), once per loader session
XL_SECS=900 XL_CMDLINE="touchscreen=1 cpufreq=1 bootcpu=7 cpus=8 gpu=1 wifi=1 adsp=1" ./xl run
./xl screenshot shot.png
./xl reboot           # back to Android
./xl with no arguments lists every command (logs, screen and sound recording, camera frames, stop, state...).
Prebuilt boot image
Every release has hackios-redwood-boot.img attached: the redwood UEFI with our loader inside, ready for fastboot boot. It contains no Apple files; the system image is still made on your machine (above).
Building from source
common/build.sh <device> runs every step that this machine can run and uses prebuilt/ for the rest.
Kernel — needs theos in ~/theos (cctools and iPhoneOS16.5.sdk) and clang lld python perl. Details: xnu/README.md.
xnu/apply.sh && xnu-deps/setup.sh && ./xnu-build.sh -j8 -k
Loader — xnuloader/build.sh (clang + lld-link, an EFI application without EDK2).
Images — REST=1 userland/build.sh (variables documented at the top of that file).
UEFI — uefi/README.md (Project Silicium port); not needed to run, prebuilt/uefi has it.
After rebuilding: tools/update-prebuilt.sh refreshes prebuilt/.
Porting to another device
common/new-device.sh <codename> path/to/device.dtb   # profile + loader platform from the phone's device tree
Then follow docs/PORTING.md: the UEFI port, the loader's platform description, the kernel's drivers, the firmware. Device profiles live in common/devices/ (redwood.conf, qemu-virt.conf, _template.conf).
How it works
fastboot boot ──► UEFI (Mu-Silicium) ──► xnuloader (EFI application)
                                           │  stays resident: USB link (fastboot protocol),
                                           │  watchdog, receives the kernel's log
                                           ▼
            XNU (BCM2837 config as the base + our platform)
              ├─ GICv3, timer, video console, return to the loader
              ├─ APFS (images in RAM, iOS volume on flash), ramfs (/private/var, /tmp)
              ├─ minicrypto instead of corecrypto, AMFI and Sandbox stand-ins (MAC policies)
              ├─ driver replacements: IOSurface, IOMobileFramebuffer, AppleKeyStore, network stack
              ├─ input: /dev/redwood-touch ◄─ Goodix GT9916 (phone) / virtio-input (QEMU)
              ├─ GPU: Adreno 642L, Wi-Fi: WCN6750 (ath11k via LinuxKPI), sound: ADSP / virtio-sound
              ▼
   iOS 16.5 launchd → logd, notifyd, cfprefsd, runningboardd, backboardd, SpringBoard, apps
              ├─ our libraries are injected into backboardd, SpringBoard and mediaserverd
              │  (virtual HID services, a few ObjC method swaps — in memory only)
              └─ mediaserverd gets our CoreAudio output device (RedwoodAudio.driver)
The iOS programs, frameworks and dyld shared cache are not changed by a single byte: what they miss is done by the kernel (driver replacements) or by a library the kernel injects with DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES (kern.exec_inject).
Layout
Path What
common/ setup.sh (workspace), build.sh / run.sh (per device), new-device.sh, devices/*.conf, ugit
xl drives the phone over USB: loader, kernel runs, logs, screenshots, screen and sound recording
xnuloader/ the loader: loader.c (UEFI application), mkpayload.py (kernel + images + arguments container)
xnu/ our XNU changes: patch, new files, apply.sh / export.sh
xnu-deps/ everything for building XNU on Linux: setup.sh, tool wrappers, stubs
xnu-build.sh, xnu-env.sh kernel build
uefi/, mkxnuimg.py the UEFI port and packing the boot image for fastboot boot
wifi/lx/ the layer on which Linux's Wi-Fi driver builds for our kernel
qemu/ QEMU runs, touch input, screenshots, stack symbolication
tools/ recording (recording.py, sound.py), UFS/flash tools, mk-ath11k.sh, new-workspace.sh, host tests
prebuilt/ built kernel, loader and UEFI pieces (NOTICES.md for the third-party code in the kernel)
docs/ screenshots, checks.md, PORTING.md
Debugging
Session log: QEMU's stdout or logs/HHMMSS-run.log from the phone.
RC_JOBS=rc.jobs.tour REST=1 userland/build.sh — an image that unlocks and opens every app of the first page.
userabort: in the log is the stack of a process that called abort(); usertrap: (with systrace=1) — crashes.
Live stacks (QEMU): qemu/touch.py stacks NAME, then qemu/symstack.py LOG NAME (needs ipsw).
How a check can lie to you: docs/checks.md.
Screenshots
From the phone's screen, one session (GL=1 REST=1, gpu=1):
Licenses
No iOS files are in the repositories: ios165/fetch.sh downloads them from Apple's CDN to your machine.
xnu/ is a derivative work of XNU and is distributed under APSL 2.0, like XNU itself; prebuilt/mach.* is the kernel built from it. It also contains ath11k (BSD-3-Clause-Clear) and FreeBSD LinuxKPI code (BSD-2-Clause): see prebuilt/NOTICES.md.
xnu/files/bsd/miscfs/apfs/libzbitmap/ and xnu-deps/build/lzbitmap/ — libzbitmap (Corellium LLC, MIT here); xnu/files/bsd/miscfs/apfs/libdeflate/ — libdeflate 1.24 (Eric Biggers, MIT, COPYING there).
ath11k, Linux and FreeBSD sources are not in the repository: tools/mk-ath11k.sh fetches pinned releases. wifi/lx/patches/*.patch are our changes to FreeBSD headers; the rest of wifi/lx/ is ours.
uefi/files/Binaries/redwood and prebuilt/uefi/SILICIUM_UEFI.fd contain UEFI drivers from the phone's Xiaomi firmware, distributed the way Project Silicium distributes them for other devices; prebuilt/uefi/mkbootimg.py — AOSP, Apache-2.0.
This repository is licensed under the Apple Public Source License 2.0: our changes to XNU are a derivative of XNU and must be, and our other code here (loader, scripts) is released under the same license. Third-party code keeps its own license, as listed above.
Team
OOSEX GANG — @oodze (founder), @netusd, @wannqn, @hxfuxyyXD. News: t.me/oosexgangdevs.

title: jank programming language - Clojure/LLVM/C++
content:
jank
Docs
Blog
Github
Slack
Discord
The native Clojure dialect with seamless C++ interop
jank is Clojure on top of C++. It has C++ interop unlike any other language. Templates, virtual functions, exceptions, overload resolution, and RAII all just work in jank. No boilerplate necessary. Just include your headers and go!
jank is a robust Clojure dialect. It offers interactive REPL-driven development powered by a Clang-based C++ JIT compiler.
Install jank
Learn jank
(ns my.app.filesystem
  (:include "boost/filesystem.hpp")
  (:refer-global :rename {boost.filesystem.file_size file-size}))

(defn file-info [file-path]
  (try
    (let [bytes (file-size (cpp/cast std.string file-path))]
      {:path file-path
       :size bytes})
    (catch boost.filesystem.filesystem_error e
      {:path file-path
       :error (.what e)})))

(file-info "/etc/passwd")
; {:path "/etc/passwd", :size 4025}

(file-info "/root/.bash_history")
; {:path "/root/.bash_history"
;  :error "boost::filesystem::file_size: Permission denied [system:13]: \"/root/.bash_history\""}
jank builds upon Clojure
Keep your existing code; unlock the native world.
jank is Clojure
jank is a full-on Clojure dialect, with C++ interop instead of Java interop. There's a :jank reader conditional for when you need it.
jank is C++
jank can include any C++ source, link to any C or C++ library, and it uses the C++ type system. jank even compiles to C++!
Cargo-inspired tooling
jank uses Leiningen-based project management and has a rich native build system. It's easy to add C and C++ dependencies to your project.
REPL and native JIT compiler
Use your favorite nREPL editor plugin. jank contains an LLVM-based JIT runtime to compile C++ code on the fly.
Native dependencies made easy
jank brings a Cargo-inspired UX to C++ and Clojure.
Easy project management
jank's native build system can find your installed native dependencies or build them from source. Adding a new dependency is a one line change.
(defproject imgui+glfw "0.1-SNAPSHOT"
  :dependencies [[org.jank-lang.commons/imgui-glfw-sys "2026.06-6"]
                 [org.jank-lang.commons/imgui-opengl2-sys "2026.06-6"]
                 [org.jank-lang.commons/gl-sys "2026.06-1"]]
  :plugins [[org.jank-lang/lein-jank "2026.06-2"]]
  :middleware [leiningen.jank/middleware]
  :main imgui+glfw.main
  :profiles {:base {:jank {:target-dir "target/debug"
                           :optimization-level 0}}
             :release {:jank {:target-dir "target/release"
                              :optimization-level 3}}})
jank is great for game dev
jank brings functional, immutable data and REPL-driven development to your game development workflow. With jank, you can reach into C++ whenever you want the extra performance. No bridges, no function/type registration, no marshalling, no callbacks.
(ns imgui+glfw.main
  (:include "GLFW/glfw3.h"
            "imgui.h" "imgui_impl_glfw.h" "imgui_impl_opengl2.h"))

(defn -main []
  (cpp/glfwInit)

  (let [window* (cpp/glfwCreateWindow 400 300
                                      "jank"
                                      cpp/nullptr cpp/nullptr)]
    (cpp/glfwMakeContextCurrent window*)
    (cpp/ImGui.CreateContext)
    (cpp/ImGui_ImplGlfw_InitForOpenGL window* true)
    (cpp/ImGui_ImplOpenGL2_Init)

    (while (cpp/! (cpp/glfwWindowShouldClose window*))
      (cpp/glfwPollEvents)
      (cpp/ImGui_ImplOpenGL2_NewFrame)
      (cpp/ImGui_ImplGlfw_NewFrame)
      (cpp/ImGui.NewFrame)

      (when (cpp/ImGui.Begin "jank")
        (cpp/ImGui.Text "Hello, jank and imgui!"))
      (cpp/ImGui.End)

      (cpp/ImGui.Render)
      (cpp/ImGui_ImplOpenGL2_RenderDrawData (cpp/ImGui.GetDrawData))
      (cpp/glfwSwapBuffers window*))

    (cpp/glfwTerminate)))
Delightful AOT compilation
Tinker all you want, but generate a compact binary when you're ready.
Startup is instantaneous.
jank's sponsors
These organizations are investing in jank's future. You can help out, too! See here.
Try jank today!
You've made it this far. Why not dive in?
Install jank
Learn jank

Project Hedra
Project Hedra is an ambitious open-world, low-poly RPG. Choose your class, explore endless procedurally generated worlds, unlock different skills and complete procedurally generated quests.
More screenshots at (Screenshots)
Timeline/Context
I started this project when I was in highschool (around 15 yo) in order to learn how OpenGL worked.
The scope creep quickly arrived and after a few years it turned into a fullfledged 3D game and game engine. The codebase has around 100k LOC and the game has first class support for Linux and Windows.
Features
The million lines of code are not in vain. The game and engine are both full of features :)
Game Features
Beatiful procedurally generated worlds
Quests and bosses
100+ items with rarities system
Skills and skill tree system with N+ skills
4 different classes with 2 specializations each ()
Procedurally placed structures generated dynamically
Fishing, crafting, etc
Trading and NPCs
Companions and pets
Beatiful soundtrack
Navigation, maps
Different dimensions
More stuff I don't recall :)
Engine Features
Fully fledged renderer using modern OpenGL
Skinned mesh rendering
Support for loading and playing generic animations
Collada (.dae) parser
Static mesh rendering
Screen space reflections
Screen space ambient occlusion
Bloom, FXAA & MSAA
Modding support
CI for automatically deploying to a Steam beta branch
Localization support
Sound support using OpenAL
Python scripting support
Module system for loading data oriented objects
Steam integration
Fully fledged UI & controls system (dropdowns, buttons, etc.) written from raw OpenGL
Dynamic shader system for reloading during runtime
Frustum culling, occlusion culling,
Mesh simplification for runtime level of detail (LOD)
Skybox support
Shadows
3D trails renderering support
Particle system using object instancing in opengl
bulletphysics integration
Chunk system for infinite worlds support
.ply parsing support
Dynamic meshing support using MarchingCubes
Custom implementation of basic C# primitives and allocators (like Lists) for supporting stack allocated lists and minimizing the automatic runtime allocations (and thus the GC).
1000+ plus test cases
Framework for mocking game components and doing integration testing on games
Image and asset compression for faster loading and smaller size
Entity component system
More stuff I don't recall :)
Interesting bits
WorldRenderer.cs. Renders the entire world in just 3 (actually it depends on how partitioned is the data buffer, but it was designed to be in 3) draw calls (water, terrain, instanced) using glMultiDrawElements.
Block.cs. Core component of the world. Read more at https://maxilevi.com/blog/procedural-meshing-hedra
Fishing.py. Written in Python as a mod script using IronPython, directly interacts with the C# API.
NativeArray.cs Implementation of an array primitive using a custom allocator. The same project provides heap based allocators as well as stac based ones using stackalloc. The idea was to minimize the automatic heap allocations (and thus avoiding the GC) during the game frames.
Interesting facts
The world is fully procedurally generated, there is no world save file. Only the player contents are saved and the world seed. The rest is created at runtime.
The world is voxel based but an isosurface extraction algorithm called Marching Cubes is applied to extract an implicit continous surface from the discrete voxels.
The name "Hedra" comes from tetrahedra which is the shape used in the original iso surface extraction algorithm I implemented Marching Tetrahedra
The game only supports loading .PLY and .DAE models, both which are in plaintext and the models have no textures. Therefore if you put this into perspective, this means I wrote a bunch of text that reads text and creates interactive images from this. I think this is pretty cool.
Screenshots
TODO add more
Code Structure
Overall Architecture
The game is a mod to a base engine. The idea of architecturing this way was to force myself to maintain the mod API up to date, therefore encouraging access to make mods.
Hedra
Basically the entire game. This includes AI logic, components, world generation, module systems, object placement and lots of other stuff.
Hedra.Engine
The core parts of the engine, this defines all the abstractions to the world. It handles rendering, sound, different base systems as well as the general windowing, game loop and platform features. The split was not done at the start so some stuff might still be outside.
Framework
Core primitives used in the engine. This includes heap and stack allocators, custom implementations of lists and arrays as well as wrappers to pointers to native and some other useful primitives
HedraTests
Test suite that
Asset Builder
Command line tool to compress the game assets into convenient binary files. Combines images, models, sound files, shaders into a single binary file with a structure designed for fast data retrieval.
Server
Once upong a time Hedra used to support multiplayer. It worked by doing UDP Hole Punching and having clients communicate P2P, this server was in charge of that. You might also see some networking remnants in the Engine code.
How to build
The build process is pretty straightforward.
Checkout all the submodules
Run the build depedencies scripts
Compile the C# solution
You can check the GitHub actions workflows for some examples on Linux and Windows.

title: Tell HN: I unknowingly broke the PHP RCE embargo. I am sorry. | Hacker News

Tell HN: I unknowingly broke the PHP RCE embargo. I am sorry.
426 points by petecooper 17 hours ago | hide | past | favorite | 182 comments
I posted here about the then-upcoming PHP RCEs related to CVE-2026-109618 & CVE-2026-109619. I appreciate this has had considerable knock-on effects with the schedule for co-ordinated disclosure, and created additional workload.
I am truly sorry. I take full responsibility for my actions.
It was not remotely my intention to cause any of the subsequent side effects.
At the time of posting, I didn't know about any embargo. My contact had told me there was no embargo, and her contact had told her the same thing.
As someone who follows the 4-weekly PHP release cycle and compiles it from source, my intention was to alert others in a similar position to be aware of the importance/urgency of the updates.
That clearly backfired in a pretty wild fashion. I have learned my lesson.
 help


creatonez 4 hours ago | next [–]

> At the time of posting, I didn't know about any embargo. My contact had told me there was no embargo, and her contact had told her the same thing.
If you're not a party to an embargo, and no one told you an embargo even exists... you should not follow the embargo. In fact, you should maybe even consider leaking basic details or challenging the embargo if you are in this situation. In your situation, they had lost information asymmetry before the news got to you. I don't know where people got the idea that unrelated third parties have to follow embargos.
Embargos are not about keeping secrets, they are about the game theory of coordinated disclosure.

nahsra 2 hours ago | root | parent | next [–]

Just FYI, "responsible disclosure" is a term that many people (like me) dislike because it carries judgment about the merits of public disclosure that are not at all obvious.
This term came from an era where companies or projects were disrespectful and dismissive towards security researchers. Those orgs were generally bad risk practitioners, and they coined the term "responsible disclosure" to mean "you send us the info and we'll do whatever we want with it, for however long we want, etc".
Many security people (like me) prefer the term "coordinated disclosure" as a way to indicate a practice where both discoverer and patcher participate in a good faith, communicative, and timely process to get things fixed for the community.
The difference can be summed up like this: if I report vulnerability X to company Y, and company Y sits on it for 3 years, that is not responsible. It is more "responsible" (especially today) to report it to the public, so they can protect themselves in a non-official-patch way, because the likelihood of bad guys knowing about it and exploiting it are approaching near-certainty.
These terms are obviously not super scientific, but I try to point out the history whenever it comes up.

saghm 3 hours ago | root | parent | next [–]

How would you even know whether you knew the facts? It sounds like what you knew was more than just consistent with there being no embargo, you were explicitly told there was no embargo. After a certain point, there's a limit to how far up the chain any of us can be expected to follow the logical chain of what we genuinely think are true, and this doesn't seem like a glaringly obvious case where you were being reckless.
We're all (well, I guess not all, but the group that's worth caring about, and I hope it's at least most) just operating the best we can on the information we have and trying to make decisions based on that. As long as you're acting in good faith on information that you had genuine basis for believing is true, it seems like it would be unreasonable to expect someone in your situation to somehow intuit that you were given false information or grossly misunderstood what sounds like a pretty straightforward declaration of fact from someone you didn't have any reason to doubt.
At the risk of some armchair paycholoanalysis because it does seem like you genuinely feel some guilt over this: I can emphathize feeling guilty about the outcome of an action that in a vacuum would not have been hard to make differently, but my experience is that those of us who have a nasty habit of beating ourselves up over things when we really don't have much blame will often recognize when on the other side that it would not be fair to hold someone else to that standard. I struggle a lot with how sometimes knowing something is true doesn't always make it feel true, and even though hearing someone else saying it doesn't magically make it all better, I still think it's valuable to hear it from someone else, so if I happen to be right about how you're feeling, nothing about all of this is your fault, and to the extent that you're able to, try not to beat yourself up over your misfortune to get caught in the middle of all this due to circumstances that realistically were outside your control.
