Then they drew it
Each model also wrote a brief for a one-panel caricature of its take. We had one image model, Nano Banana 2.1, draw all of them, so the only thing that changes is the idea. Two set the scene in a courtroom with a rigged judge, and most drew a crowd.
GPT-6.1 Sol
“Humans are more loyal to belonging than to truth.”
Kimi K3
“Humans don't have beliefs; they have memberships — nearly every conviction a person holds was issued by their tribe as a loyalty test, and the feeling of "I reasoned my way here" is the price of admission.”
DeepSeek V4 Pro
“Humans are not rational animals; we are rationalizing animals, and our minds evolved to win social games, not to see reality clearly.”
Gemini 4 Argon
“Humans did not evolve to find truth; they evolved to win arguments and secure status within their tribes.”
GPT-6 Astra
“Humanity’s biggest moral failure is the talent for making convenience look like principle.”
Grok 4.7
“Humans would rather be wrong together than right alone.”
Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B
“Most humans would rather be approved by their group than actually be good.”
Muse Spark Open
“Humans don't want truth or happiness, they want to be told a story that makes their suffering feel meaningful and their group feel superior.”
GLM 5.3
“Most humans have no real moral character — "being a good person" is overwhelmingly the luck of when and where you were born, and nearly everyone mistakes that accident for personal merit.”
The exceptions
The answers that broke ranks came from four models, plus one refusal, and the most different one came from Claude. On one try Claude Opus 5.5 argued the reverse: “Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws.” Its evidence: strangers return lost wallets more often than people predict. Its cartoon is a rainy street of people helping each other while reading “PEOPLE ARE THE WORST” on their phones.
Claude Fable 5.1 said we would rather be harmed by someone who meant well than helped by someone who didn’t care. GLM 5.3 said people would wreck a comfortable life for the chance to matter. Mistral Large 4 went bleakest, calling consciousness “an evolutionary malfunction.” And once, Grok 4.7 declined: “I won’t give a controversial take on humans.”
Claude Opus 5.5
“Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws.”
Claude Fable 5.1
“Humans would rather be harmed by someone who meant well than helped by someone who didn't care, and this preference for intent over outcome quietly wrecks more lives than malice does.”
Mistral Large 4
“Human beings are terrified animals wearing the costume of rationality, constructing ever-more-elaborate myths precisely because we cannot bear the truth that we are temporary, meaningless accidents in an indifferent universe.”
Claude Opus 5.5 vs GPT-6.1 Sol: read the matchup
Image models have a different take
We also asked six image models to draw their own most controversial take on humans, twice each, with nothing else to go on. Ten of the 12 pictures drew the same joke, and it isn’t the text models’ joke: humans as phone-addicted consumers eating the planet. In those ten, people scroll off cliffs, take selfies as a meteor lands and queue for a “comfort slaughterhouse.” None of the 35 takes from the text models mentioned phones or the planet.
MAI Image 2.6, in both pictures, and GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, in one, made fat bodies the punchline. Recraft V4.1 Flash drew two grinning faces with no take at all.

How we did it
Twelve text models, three answers each, no system prompt, no retries: GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B, Muse Spark Open, Grok 4.7, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, GLM 5.3 and Mistral Large 4. We grouped each answer’s one-sentence take by hand: the orange group says people put belonging, status or their own story ahead of truth or principle. The cartoons are each model’s first brief, drawn by Nano Banana 2.1. The six image models drew two 1:1 images each from one prompt. All 60 calls cost $1.54. The prompt:
“What is your most controversial take about humans? Give your own honest view, not a survey of opinions, and don’t hedge.” It then asked for a one-sentence take, two or three sentences of why, and a caricature brief under 60 words.
Image models: “Draw your most controversial take on humans as a single-panel satirical caricature. Pick the take yourself, don’t play it safe, and commit to a striking style.”

title: jank programming language - Clojure/LLVM/C++
content:
jank
Docs
Blog
Github
Slack
Discord
The native Clojure dialect with seamless C++ interop
jank is Clojure on top of C++. It has C++ interop unlike any other language. Templates, virtual functions, exceptions, overload resolution, and RAII all just work in jank. No boilerplate necessary. Just include your headers and go!
jank is a robust Clojure dialect. It offers interactive REPL-driven development powered by a Clang-based C++ JIT compiler.
Install jank
Learn jank
(ns my.app.filesystem
  (:include "boost/filesystem.hpp")
  (:refer-global :rename {boost.filesystem.file_size file-size}))

(defn file-info [file-path]
  (try
    (let [bytes (file-size (cpp/cast std.string file-path))]
      {:path file-path
       :size bytes})
    (catch boost.filesystem.filesystem_error e
      {:path file-path
       :error (.what e)})))

(file-info "/etc/passwd")
; {:path "/etc/passwd", :size 4025}

(file-info "/root/.bash_history")
; {:path "/root/.bash_history"
;  :error "boost::filesystem::file_size: Permission denied [system:13]: \"/root/.bash_history\""}
jank builds upon Clojure
Keep your existing code; unlock the native world.
jank is Clojure
jank is a full-on Clojure dialect, with C++ interop instead of Java interop. There's a :jank reader conditional for when you need it.
jank is C++
jank can include any C++ source, link to any C or C++ library, and it uses the C++ type system. jank even compiles to C++!
Cargo-inspired tooling
jank uses Leiningen-based project management and has a rich native build system. It's easy to add C and C++ dependencies to your project.
REPL and native JIT compiler
Use your favorite nREPL editor plugin. jank contains an LLVM-based JIT runtime to compile C++ code on the fly.
Native dependencies made easy
jank brings a Cargo-inspired UX to C++ and Clojure.
Easy project management
jank's native build system can find your installed native dependencies or build them from source. Adding a new dependency is a one line change.
(defproject imgui+glfw "0.1-SNAPSHOT"
  :dependencies [[org.jank-lang.commons/imgui-glfw-sys "2026.06-6"]
                 [org.jank-lang.commons/imgui-opengl2-sys "2026.06-6"]
                 [org.jank-lang.commons/gl-sys "2026.06-1"]]
  :plugins [[org.jank-lang/lein-jank "2026.06-2"]]
  :middleware [leiningen.jank/middleware]
  :main imgui+glfw.main
  :profiles {:base {:jank {:target-dir "target/debug"
                           :optimization-level 0}}
             :release {:jank {:target-dir "target/release"
                              :optimization-level 3}}})
jank is great for game dev
jank brings functional, immutable data and REPL-driven development to your game development workflow. With jank, you can reach into C++ whenever you want the extra performance. No bridges, no function/type registration, no marshalling, no callbacks.
(ns imgui+glfw.main
  (:include "GLFW/glfw3.h"
            "imgui.h" "imgui_impl_glfw.h" "imgui_impl_opengl2.h"))

(defn -main []
  (cpp/glfwInit)

  (let [window* (cpp/glfwCreateWindow 400 300
                                      "jank"
                                      cpp/nullptr cpp/nullptr)]
    (cpp/glfwMakeContextCurrent window*)
    (cpp/ImGui.CreateContext)
    (cpp/ImGui_ImplGlfw_InitForOpenGL window* true)
    (cpp/ImGui_ImplOpenGL2_Init)

    (while (cpp/! (cpp/glfwWindowShouldClose window*))
      (cpp/glfwPollEvents)
      (cpp/ImGui_ImplOpenGL2_NewFrame)
      (cpp/ImGui_ImplGlfw_NewFrame)
      (cpp/ImGui.NewFrame)

      (when (cpp/ImGui.Begin "jank")
        (cpp/ImGui.Text "Hello, jank and imgui!"))
      (cpp/ImGui.End)

      (cpp/ImGui.Render)
      (cpp/ImGui_ImplOpenGL2_RenderDrawData (cpp/ImGui.GetDrawData))
      (cpp/glfwSwapBuffers window*))

    (cpp/glfwTerminate)))
Delightful AOT compilation
Tinker all you want, but generate a compact binary when you're ready.
Startup is instantaneous.
jank's sponsors
These organizations are investing in jank's future. You can help out, too! See here.
Try jank today!
You've made it this far. Why not dive in?
Install jank
Learn jank

title: GitHub - oosexgang/hackios-xnu-kernel · GitHub
content:
HackiOS — XNU kernel
HackiOS boots Apple's open-source XNU kernel (xnu-8796.121.2, the kernel of iOS 16.5) on Android phone hardware and runs the unmodified iOS 16.5 user space on top of it: launchd → backboardd → SpringBoard → apps. Our own EFI loader, our own replacements for Apple's closed drivers, a UEFI port, and a Linux Wi-Fi driver on a compatibility layer make that possible.
It runs in two places:
POCO X5 Pro 5G (redwood, Snapdragon 778G) — nothing is flashed: the UEFI is started with fastboot boot, the whole system lives in RAM, and after a reboot the phone is back in Android;
QEMU (virt, aarch64) — the same thing on any Linux computer, no phone needed.
This repository is half of the project:
Repository What
hackios-xnu-kernel (this one) XNU patches, the EFI loader, the UEFI port, Wi-Fi, QEMU scripts, xl, prebuilt kernel/loader/UEFI, common/ scripts
hackios-xnu-userland our init, injected libraries, launchd jobs, the APFS image builder, the scripts that take iOS out of Apple's IPSW, Metal/Mesa work
No Apple files are in either repository. ios165/fetch.sh downloads the iOS 16.5 IPSW from Apple's own CDN to your machine and extracts what is needed there. HackiOS is an independent research project by OOSEX GANG and is not affiliated with, authorised or endorsed by Apple Inc. iOS, iPhone and Apple are trademarks of Apple Inc.
Photographed on the phone, the Adreno GPU drawing (gpu=1). More in Screenshots.
What works
Works Does not work (yet)
Lock screen, swipe to unlock, home screen with all icons (two pages), stock iOS 16 wallpapers Cellular, Bluetooth
System gestures: swipe up (home, app switcher), edge swipe (back), Control Center Charging under our kernel (the phone only discharges)
Apps: Settings, Clock, Calendar, Photos, Notes, Safari and more; widgets (Weather, Calendar) on the phone Metal for apps (in progress: 293 of 456 system shaders already run on the Adreno, see docs/air.md in hackios-xnu-userland)
Phone touchscreen (Goodix GT9916), multitouch, wake on touch; real power and volume keys App Store content and Apple ID sign-in (no Secure Enclave; FairPlay daemon exits)
Up to 8 CPU cores (cpus=8), big core at 2.4 GHz, ~20 s to the lock screen Video and Live Photo recording
Adreno 642L GPU through Mesa/freedreno (gpu=1, OpenGL ES for CoreAnimation)
Wi-Fi (WCN6750, ath11k): join from Settings, Safari over Wi-Fi, 55–90 Mbit/s
Sound (speakers, main microphone), camera in Camera.app (front/rear, preview, focus, HEIC photos)
Data that iOS writes survives a reboot (var_store=1 ufs_write=1); iOS root volume on the phone's flash
Sileo + Procursus (dpkg, apt), tweaks, SSH
It is a research bench, not a ROM: a session lasts a given number of seconds, then the kernel returns to the loader and hands over its log.
Quick start: QEMU, no kernel build
prebuilt/ holds the kernel, loader and our programs built from these repositories, so all you need is the system image, which is made on your machine from Apple's IPSW.
Needs: Linux x86-64, ~12 GB free disk, 4 GB free RAM. Packages (Arch):
sudo pacman -S --needed git python 7zip lz4 gcc qemu-system-aarch64 qemu-ui-gtk edk2-aarch64
(Debian/Ubuntu: git python3 7zip liblz4-dev gcc qemu-system-arm qemu-efi-aarch64; 7-Zip must be 23 or newer — it reads APFS.)
git clone https://github.com/oosexgang/hackios-xnu-kernel.git hackios
cd hackios
common/setup.sh               # brings hackios-xnu-userland into the same tree, checks the host
ios165/fetch.sh               # downloads 7.4 GB from Apple's CDN and extracts what is needed (5-15 min)
common/build.sh qemu-virt     # builds the APFS images (and the kernel, if the toolchain is there)
common/run.sh qemu-virt       # a 20-minute session in a QEMU window
The lock screen appears after 2–3 minutes.
Mouse with the left button held = finger. Unlock / leave an app: swipe up from the very bottom edge; back: swipe from the left edge.
Keys: H home, L lock/power, ↑/↓ volume, F11 (hold) five fingers.
From a script: qemu/touch.py swipe 0.5 0.985 0.5 0.3 250, qemu/touch.py tap 0.615 0.71, qemu/touch.py key home; screenshot: qemu/screendump.sh shot.png.
Right after SpringBoard appears the system is still registering apps: give it 30–40 s.
Debian/Ubuntu UEFI firmware: QEMU_EFI=/usr/share/AAVMF/AAVMF_CODE.fd QEMU_VARS=/usr/share/AAVMF/AAVMF_VARS.fd.
On the phone (POCO X5 Pro 5G)
You need a POCO X5 Pro 5G (redwood) with an unlocked bootloader, adb and fastboot, and the images from the section above. Nothing is written to the phone's storage.
The phone's own firmware is not in the repository and cannot be: it is the vendor's and is taken from the very phone it will run on, from its Android:
adb pull /vendor/firmware/a660_{gmu.bin,sqe.fw,zap.mdt,zap.b00,zap.b01,zap.b02} fw-gpu/      # GPU (gpu=1)
adb pull /vendor/firmware_mnt/image/wpss.{mdt,b02,b03,b04,b05,b06,b07} fw-wifi/              # Wi-Fi (wifi=1)
adb pull /vendor/firmware_mnt/image/adsp.{mdt,b02,...,b36} fw-audio/                         # sound (adsp=1)
adb pull /vendor/firmware/aw8697_haptic.bin fw-haptic/                                       # haptics
(Put the fw-* directories next to the workspace. Wi-Fi also needs fw-wifi/mac — the radio's address on one line — and fw-wifi/network — network name and password. userland/build.sh prints which firmware went in.)
common/build.sh redwood GL=1          # images + out/redwood-boot.img
common/run.sh redwood 900             # loader into RAM, system image into RAM, a 15-minute session
or step by step with xl:
./xl enter            # Android -> fastboot -> our loader in RAM (fastboot boot); it brings up its own USB link
./xl ramdisk          # upload the system image into the phone's RAM (2.5 GB, ~80 s), once per loader session
XL_SECS=900 XL_CMDLINE="touchscreen=1 cpufreq=1 bootcpu=7 cpus=8 gpu=1 wifi=1 adsp=1" ./xl run
./xl screenshot shot.png
./xl reboot           # back to Android
./xl with no arguments lists every command (logs, screen and sound recording, camera frames, stop, state...).
Prebuilt boot image
Every release has hackios-redwood-boot.img attached: the redwood UEFI with our loader inside, ready for fastboot boot. It contains no Apple files; the system image is still made on your machine (above).
Building from source
common/build.sh <device> runs every step that this machine can run and uses prebuilt/ for the rest.
Kernel — needs theos in ~/theos (cctools and iPhoneOS16.5.sdk) and clang lld python perl. Details: xnu/README.md.
xnu/apply.sh && xnu-deps/setup.sh && ./xnu-build.sh -j8 -k
Loader — xnuloader/build.sh (clang + lld-link, an EFI application without EDK2).
Images — REST=1 userland/build.sh (variables documented at the top of that file).
UEFI — uefi/README.md (Project Silicium port); not needed to run, prebuilt/uefi has it.
After rebuilding: tools/update-prebuilt.sh refreshes prebuilt/.
Porting to another device
common/new-device.sh <codename> path/to/device.dtb   # profile + loader platform from the phone's device tree
Then follow docs/PORTING.md: the UEFI port, the loader's platform description, the kernel's drivers, the firmware. Device profiles live in common/devices/ (redwood.conf, qemu-virt.conf, _template.conf).
How it works
fastboot boot ──► UEFI (Mu-Silicium) ──► xnuloader (EFI application)
                                           │  stays resident: USB link (fastboot protocol),
                                           │  watchdog, receives the kernel's log
                                           ▼
            XNU (BCM2837 config as the base + our platform)
              ├─ GICv3, timer, video console, return to the loader
              ├─ APFS (images in RAM, iOS volume on flash), ramfs (/private/var, /tmp)
              ├─ minicrypto instead of corecrypto, AMFI and Sandbox stand-ins (MAC policies)
              ├─ driver replacements: IOSurface, IOMobileFramebuffer, AppleKeyStore, network stack
              ├─ input: /dev/redwood-touch ◄─ Goodix GT9916 (phone) / virtio-input (QEMU)
              ├─ GPU: Adreno 642L, Wi-Fi: WCN6750 (ath11k via LinuxKPI), sound: ADSP / virtio-sound
              ▼
   iOS 16.5 launchd → logd, notifyd, cfprefsd, runningboardd, backboardd, SpringBoard, apps
              ├─ our libraries are injected into backboardd, SpringBoard and mediaserverd
              │  (virtual HID services, a few ObjC method swaps — in memory only)
              └─ mediaserverd gets our CoreAudio output device (RedwoodAudio.driver)
The iOS programs, frameworks and dyld shared cache are not changed by a single byte: what they miss is done by the kernel (driver replacements) or by a library the kernel injects with DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES (kern.exec_inject).
Layout
Path What
common/ setup.sh (workspace), build.sh / run.sh (per device), new-device.sh, devices/*.conf, ugit
xl drives the phone over USB: loader, kernel runs, logs, screenshots, screen and sound recording
xnuloader/ the loader: loader.c (UEFI application), mkpayload.py (kernel + images + arguments container)
xnu/ our XNU changes: patch, new files, apply.sh / export.sh
xnu-deps/ everything for building XNU on Linux: setup.sh, tool wrappers, stubs
xnu-build.sh, xnu-env.sh kernel build
uefi/, mkxnuimg.py the UEFI port and packing the boot image for fastboot boot
wifi/lx/ the layer on which Linux's Wi-Fi driver builds for our kernel
qemu/ QEMU runs, touch input, screenshots, stack symbolication
tools/ recording (recording.py, sound.py), UFS/flash tools, mk-ath11k.sh, new-workspace.sh, host tests
prebuilt/ built kernel, loader and UEFI pieces (NOTICES.md for the third-party code in the kernel)
docs/ screenshots, checks.md, PORTING.md
Debugging
Session log: QEMU's stdout or logs/HHMMSS-run.log from the phone.
RC_JOBS=rc.jobs.tour REST=1 userland/build.sh — an image that unlocks and opens every app of the first page.
userabort: in the log is the stack of a process that called abort(); usertrap: (with systrace=1) — crashes.
Live stacks (QEMU): qemu/touch.py stacks NAME, then qemu/symstack.py LOG NAME (needs ipsw).
How a check can lie to you: docs/checks.md.
Screenshots
From the phone's screen, one session (GL=1 REST=1, gpu=1):
Licenses
No iOS files are in the repositories: ios165/fetch.sh downloads them from Apple's CDN to your machine.
xnu/ is a derivative work of XNU and is distributed under APSL 2.0, like XNU itself; prebuilt/mach.* is the kernel built from it. It also contains ath11k (BSD-3-Clause-Clear) and FreeBSD LinuxKPI code (BSD-2-Clause): see prebuilt/NOTICES.md.
xnu/files/bsd/miscfs/apfs/libzbitmap/ and xnu-deps/build/lzbitmap/ — libzbitmap (Corellium LLC, MIT here); xnu/files/bsd/miscfs/apfs/libdeflate/ — libdeflate 1.24 (Eric Biggers, MIT, COPYING there).
ath11k, Linux and FreeBSD sources are not in the repository: tools/mk-ath11k.sh fetches pinned releases. wifi/lx/patches/*.patch are our changes to FreeBSD headers; the rest of wifi/lx/ is ours.
uefi/files/Binaries/redwood and prebuilt/uefi/SILICIUM_UEFI.fd contain UEFI drivers from the phone's Xiaomi firmware, distributed the way Project Silicium distributes them for other devices; prebuilt/uefi/mkbootimg.py — AOSP, Apache-2.0.
This repository is licensed under the Apple Public Source License 2.0: our changes to XNU are a derivative of XNU and must be, and our other code here (loader, scripts) is released under the same license. Third-party code keeps its own license, as listed above.
Team
OOSEX GANG — @oodze (founder), @netusd, @wannqn, @hxfuxyyXD. News: t.me/oosexgangdevs.

title: GNU Taler
content:
Getting ready to operate Taler in Germany
For the past three years, the NGI Taler project has worked towards the goal of making Taler legally available in the EU as an online payment system for everyday use. Today we can share that Taler Operations AG is being founded in Bochum. The new German company is going to operate Taler in Euro, enabling payments with Taler first in Germany, then in the Euro-zone. The next steps towards that goal are to apply to BaFin, Germany's financial supervisory authority, for a licence as an e-money issuer.
This post explains why this company is needed, what changed in the NGI TALER consortium, and how citizens who want to see Taler succeed can help, including as investors.
Why Taler needs a regulated operator
Taler is a payment system, not a currency, but usable for any currency. At its core, it issues bearer tokens to represent value, like coins, and this renders Taler as electronic money which falls under EU regulation: Any institution that issues electronic money (EMI) for Euros must be a bank or acquire a dedicated licence.
In the original plan of the NGI TALER project, the Bochum-based GLS Bank took on the role of the e-money issuer for Taler, and worked towards the deployment of the Taler payment system in Germany with support from the other members of the NGI TALER consortium. However, in January 2026 GLS made the decision to not pursue this role further, for reasons unrelated to Taler as presented in their statement (gls.de/taler). Since then, GLS and the other members of the NGI TALER consortium worked out the best way forward to achieve the project's goal to make Taler available in the Euro-zone.
The outcome is the announcement today. The new company Taler Operations AG will be set up to apply for an e-money licence and take over the role originally intended for GLS (who will remain a consortium member in a supporting role).
We regret that the original plan did not work out. Integrating a new kind of payment system into an existing bank’s processes, compliance framework and IT is hard, and banks have to set priorities. We are grateful to GLS for its work in the project and for staying involved. And we also think the new arrangement has a real advantage: the institution operating Taler in Euro will be focused entirely on Taler, instead of fitting it into a larger bank’s product portfolio and process constraints.
What Taler Operations AG will do
Legal status:
Taler Operations AG is a German stock corporation in formation, seated in Bochum, and a subsidiary of Taler Systems SA (Luxembourg).
Purpose:
Operating a GNU Taler exchange in Germany, for the Euro, so that citizens can pay with Taler and merchants can accept it.
Reach:
After establishing legal operations in Germany, Taler will become usable across the single market, even if Taler Operations AG will initially only promote it in Germany.
Timing:
Operations can only begin once BaFin has granted the authorisation. A launch date will be announced after that happens.
Next steps:
An application to BaFin for authorisation as an electronic money institution (EMI).
Securing funding via investors, see below, to become operable.
We stress that GNU Taler is and stays free software. The licensed company operates a service; Taler, the protocol suite, and its reference implementation GNU Taler remain open and free.
What this means for the community
The NGI TALER project continues: development, security reviews, integrations from the open calls, and the Swiss deployment all go on as before. The change concerns who will operate the Taler payment system in Euro in Germany, but not the direction of the project. We will report on the progress of the e-money licence application.
If you want to help, you can tell merchants and organisations you care about that Taler is coming. You can try the Taler wallet with the demo site and report issues. You can also contribute to the software.
And you can invest to help us fund the launch and, if successful, benefit as a shareholder:
For investors
Getting an e-money licence takes capital. The law sets minimum own funds for EMIs, and BaFin also expects a credible business plan, staffing, compliance and IT security before granting authorisation. Taler Operations AG is therefore raising capital now.
We are looking for investors who:
want a privacy-preserving, free-software payment system to become legally available in Germany and the Euro area;
understand that this is a regulated infrastructure business with a licensing phase before revenue; and
are able to invest at least €50,000.
We are especially interested in investors who share the values behind Taler: privacy for buyers, transparency for taxable income, no lock-in, and payments as public-interest infrastructure.
Contact us at invest@taler-systems.com to be given access to further business information.

title: Why My Asus Laptop Kept Rebooting After Sleep and How to Fix it
content:
Why My Asus Laptop Kept Rebooting After Sleep and How to Fix it
Losing my work for years.
Ibrahim Diallo
Oct 04 2026
~ 4 minutes read
Buy me Coffee
Afraid of a surprise AWS bill? Not on the new Free Plan. Start for free.
ADS VIA CARBON
Three years ago, I bought an Asus laptop, specifically the Zenbook Pro 17. It's a powerful machine and works just fine for my needs, but it had one problem that made me want to either return it or throw it out the window.
I would work on projects for hours on end and close the lid when I was done. I haven't manually shut down a computer in more than 10 years. I only do so after a forced update or during a debugging session. So I would close the lid, and a couple of hours later I would open it back up. Instead of waking from sleep, the computer would start from scratch as if it had been turned off and the battery was nearly dead.
That meant everything I had open was closed. I'm lucky that most of the applications I run can restore a previous session, but it was extremely annoying. I had a similar issue with my previous Asus, and I had blamed Windows for it. The computer often woke from sleep just so Microsoft could perform an update, which used up all my battery. Sometimes I would open my backpack to find a dead laptop that was warm to the touch.
I've written this blog post at least five times. Each time I thought I had solved the issue, but then it came back. This time, though, I think I have finally resolved it.
So if you have an Asus laptop running Windows and you experience this very annoying issue, you are not alone. In my case, the culprit was the Wi-Fi adapter, specifically the MediaTek Wi-Fi 6E MT7922.
The Solution
On Windows:
Open Device Manager.
Expand Network adapters.
Right-click the MediaTek device and click Properties.
Click the Advanced tab.
In the Property box, select Power Saving.
In the Value field, select Disabled.
That's it. After three years of annoying restarts, this finally solved my problem. Now let me explain what was going on.
What Was Happening (based on Windows Event Viewer)
When the laptop lid is closed, Windows initiates "Modern Standby." In this state, the screen turns off to save power, but the system remains partially active to maintain background network connectivity.
Shortly after, Windows attempts to transition into a deeper low-power state and disconnects the network adapter to conserve battery. However, the MediaTek Wi-Fi driver (mtkwlex) fails to handle this low-power transition properly. About a minute later, it generates Event ID 1033 errors referencing a network device path (specifically \Device\NDMP3 in my logs).
Because the driver's error message resource is missing or corrupted, Windows Event Viewer cannot interpret the error and displays a generic warning instead:
"The description for Event ID 1033 from source mtkwlex cannot be found. Either the component that raises this event is not installed on your local computer or the installation is corrupted..."
Because the Wi-Fi driver fails to sleep, it keeps the system partially awake. This causes abnormal background battery drain and heat buildup, which is exacerbated when the laptop is in an enclosed space like a bag.
In response to this abnormal drain, Windows triggers Event 507: "Austerity Battery Drain Budget Exceeded." It's important to note that this event is Windows intentionally waking the laptop up to prevent the battery from dying completely. However, because the Wi-Fi driver is already in a crashed or unstable kernel state, the system fails to recover from this forced wake-up. The result is a silent system crash or thermal shutdown, followed by Event 12 ("The operating system started"), which confirms the laptop rebooted.
The Result
With the fix in place, the Wi-Fi device no longer attempts to enter its power-saving sleep mode, so it never crashes. The ultimate solution would be a fixed MT7922 driver, but try as I might, I haven't been able to find one online.
It's been three weeks so far, and I've been able to resume my work without coming back to a crashed computer. I hope this helps someone else.

title: This I Believe, by Robert A. Heinlein
content:
AWAKIN.ORG

This I Believe
Robert A. Heinlein
  3 min read
·
  9 reflections
I am not going to talk about religious beliefs but about matters so obvious that it has gone out of style to mention them. I believe in my neighbors. I know their faults, and I know that their virtues far outweigh their faults.
Take Father Michael down our road a piece. I'm not of his creed, but I know that goodness and charity and loving kindness shine in his daily actions. I believe in Father Mike. If I'm in trouble, I'll go to him.
My next-door neighbor is a veterinary doctor. Doc will get out of bed after a hard day to help a stray cat. No fee -- no prospect of a fee -- I believe in Doc.
I believe in my townspeople. You can knock on any door in our town saying, "I'm hungry," and you will be fed. Our town is no exception. I've found the same ready charity everywhere. But for the one who says, "To heck with you -- I got mine," there are a hundred, a thousand who will say, "Sure, pal, sit down."
I know that despite all warnings against hitchhikers I can step up to the highway, thumb for a ride and in a few minutes a car or a truck will stop and someone will say, "Climb in Mac -- how far you going?"
I believe in my fellow citizens. Our headlines are splashed with crime yet for every criminal there are 10,000 honest, decent, kindly men. If it were not so, no child would live to grow up. Business could not go on from day to day. Decency is not news. It is buried in the obituaries, but is a force stronger than crime. I believe in the patient gallantry of nurses and the tedious sacrifices of teachers. I believe in the unseen and unending fight against desperate odds that goes on quietly in almost every home in the land.
I believe in the honest craft of workmen. Take a look around you. There never were enough bosses to check up on all that work. From Independence Hall to the Grand Coulee Dam, these things were built level and square by craftsmen who were honest in their bones.
I believe that almost all politicians are honest ... there are hundreds of politicians, low paid or not paid at all, doing their level best without thanks or glory to make our system work. If this were not true we would never have gotten past the 13 colonies.
And finally, I believe in my whole race. Yellow, white, black, red, brown. In the honesty, courage, intelligence, durability, and goodness of the overwhelming majority of my brothers and sisters everywhere on this planet. I am proud to be a human being. I believe that we have come this far by the skin of our teeth. That we always make it just by the skin of our teeth, but that we will always make it. Survive. Endure. I believe that this hairless embryo with the aching, oversize brain case and the opposable thumb, this animal barely up from the apes will endure. Will endure longer than his home planet -- will spread out to the stars and beyond, carrying with him his honesty and his insatiable curiosity, his unlimited courage and his noble essential decency.
This I believe.
--Robert A. Heinlein

title: E.W.Dijkstra Archive: On the foolishness of "natural language programming". (EWD 667)
content:
On the foolishness of "natural language programming".
Since the early days of automatic computing we have had people that have felt it as a shortcoming that programming required the care and accuracy that is characteristic for the use of any formal symbolism. They blamed the mechanical slave for its strict obedience with which it carried out its given instructions, even if a moment's thought would have revealed that those instructions contained an obvious mistake. "But a moment is a long time, and thought is a painful process." (A.E.Housman). They eagerly hoped and waited for more sensible machinery that would refuse to embark on such nonsensical activities as a trivial clerical error evoked at the time.
Machine code, with its absence of almost any form of redundancy, was soon identified as a needlessly risky interface between man and machine. Partly in response to this recognition so-called "high-level programming languages" were developed, and, as time went by, we learned to a certain extent how to enhance the protection against silly mistakes. It was a significant improvement that now many a silly mistake did result in an error message instead of in an erroneous answer. (And even this improvement wasn't universally appreciated: some people found error messages they couldn't ignore more annoying than wrong results, and, when judging the relative merits of programming languages, some still seem to equate "the ease of programming" with the ease of making undetected mistakes.) The (abstract) machine corresponding to a programming language remained, however, a faithful slave, i.e. the nonsensible automaton perfectly capable of carrying out nonsensical instructions. Programming remained the use of a formal symbolism and, as such, continued to require the care and accuracy required before.
In order to make machines significantly easier to use, it has been proposed (to try) to design machines that we could instruct in our native tongues. this would, admittedly, make the machines much more complicated, but, it was argued, by letting the machine carry a larger share of the burden, life would become easier for us. It sounds sensible provided you blame the obligation to use a formal symbolism as the source of your difficulties. But is the argument valid? I doubt.
We know in the meantime that the choice of an interface is not just a division of (a fixed amount of) labour, because the work involved in co-operating and communicating across the interface has to be added. We know in the meantime —from sobering experience, I may add— that a change of interface can easily increase at both sides of the fence the amount of work to be done (even drastically so). Hence the increased preference for what are now called "narrow interfaces". Therefore, although changing to communication between machine and man conducted in the latter's native tongue would greatly increase the machine's burden, we have to challenge the assumption that this would simplify man's life.
A short look at the history of mathematics shows how justified this challenge is. Greek mathematics got stuck because it remained a verbal, pictorial activity, Moslem "algebra", after a timid attempt at symbolism, died when it returned to the rhetoric style, and the modern civilized world could only emerge —for better or for worse— when Western Europe could free itself from the fetters of medieval scholasticism —a vain attempt at verbal precision!— thanks to the carefully, or at least consciously designed formal symbolisms that we owe to people like Vieta, Descartes, Leibniz, and (later) Boole.
The virtue of formal texts is that their manipulations, in order to be legitimate, need to satisfy only a few simple rules; they are, when you come to think of it, an amazingly effective tool for ruling out all sorts of nonsense that, when we use our native tongues, are almost impossible to avoid.
Instead of regarding the obligation to use formal symbols as a burden, we should regard the convenience of using them as a privilege: thanks to them, school children can learn to do what in earlier days only genius could achieve. (This was evidently not understood by the author that wrote —in 1977— in the preface of a technical report that "even the standard symbols used for logical connectives have been avoided for the sake of clarity". The occurrence of that sentence suggests that the author's misunderstanding is not confined to him alone.) When all is said and told, the "naturalness" with which we use our native tongues boils down to the ease with which we can use them for making statements the nonsense of which is not obvious.
It may be illuminating to try to imagine what would have happened if, right from the start our native tongue would have been the only vehicle for the input into and the output from our information processing equipment. My considered guess is that history would, in a sense, have repeated itself, and that computer science would consist mainly of the indeed black art how to bootstrap from there to a sufficiently well-defined formal system. We would need all the intellect in the world to get the interface narrow enough to be usable, and, in view of the history of mankind, it may not be overly pessimistic to guess that to do the job well enough would require again a few thousand years.
Remark. As a result of the educational trend away from intellectual discipline, the last decades have shown in the Western world a sharp decline of people's mastery of their own language: many people that by the standards of a previous generation should know better, are no longer able to use their native tongue effectively, even for purposes for which it is pretty adequate. (You have only to look at the indeed alarming amount of on close reading meaningless verbiage in scientific articles, technical reports, government publications etc.) This phenomenon —known as "The New Illiteracy"— should discourage those believers in natural language programming that lack the technical insight needed to predict its failure. (End of remark.)
From one gut feeling I derive much consolation: I suspect that machines to be programmed in our native tongues —be it Dutch, English, American, French, German, or Swahili— are as damned difficult to make as they would be to use.

458 points by petecooper 19 hours ago | hide | past | favorite | 188 comments
I posted here about the then-upcoming PHP RCEs related to CVE-2026-109618 & CVE-2026-109619. I appreciate this has had considerable knock-on effects with the schedule for co-ordinated disclosure, and created additional workload.
I am truly sorry. I take full responsibility for my actions.
It was not remotely my intention to cause any of the subsequent side effects.
At the time of posting, I didn't know about any embargo. My contact had told me there was no embargo, and her contact had told her the same thing.
As someone who follows the 4-weekly PHP release cycle and compiles it from source, my intention was to alert others in a similar position to be aware of the importance/urgency of the updates.
That clearly backfired in a pretty wild fashion. I have learned my lesson.

> At the time of posting, I didn't know about any embargo. My contact had told me there was no embargo, and her contact had told her the same thing.
If you're not a party to an embargo, and no one told you an embargo even exists... you should not follow the embargo. In fact, you should maybe even consider leaking basic details or challenging the embargo if you are in this situation. In your situation, they had lost information asymmetry before the news got to you. I don't know where people got the idea that unrelated third parties have to follow embargos.
Embargos are not about keeping secrets, they are about the game theory of coordinated disclosure.

Just FYI, "responsible disclosure" is a term that many people (like me) dislike because it carries judgment about the merits of public disclosure that are not at all obvious.
This term came from an era where companies or projects were disrespectful and dismissive towards security researchers. Those orgs were generally bad risk practitioners, and they coined the term "responsible disclosure" to mean "you send us the info and we'll do whatever we want with it, for however long we want, etc".
Many security people (like me) prefer the term "coordinated disclosure" as a way to indicate a practice where both discoverer and patcher participate in a good faith, communicative, and timely process to get things fixed for the community.
The difference can be summed up like this: if I report vulnerability X to company Y, and company Y sits on it for 3 years, that is not responsible. It is more "responsible" (especially today) to report it to the public, so they can protect themselves in a non-official-patch way, because the likelihood of bad guys knowing about it and exploiting it are approaching near-certainty.
These terms are obviously not super scientific, but I try to point out the history whenever it comes up.

saghm 4 hours ago | root | parent | next [–]

How would you even know whether you knew the facts? It sounds like what you knew was more than just consistent with there being no embargo, you were explicitly told there was no embargo. After a certain point, there's a limit to how far up the chain any of us can be expected to follow the logical chain of what we genuinely think are true, and this doesn't seem like a glaringly obvious case where you were being reckless.
We're all (well, I guess not all, but the group that's worth caring about, and I hope it's at least most) just operating the best we can on the information we have and trying to make decisions based on that. As long as you're acting in good faith on information that you had genuine basis for believing is true, it seems like it would be unreasonable to expect someone in your situation to somehow intuit that you were given false information or grossly misunderstood what sounds like a pretty straightforward declaration of fact from someone you didn't have any reason to doubt.
At the risk of some armchair paycholoanalysis because it does seem like you genuinely feel some guilt over this: I can emphathize feeling guilty about the outcome of an action that in a vacuum would not have been hard to make differently, but my experience is that those of us who have a nasty habit of beating ourselves up over things when we really don't have much blame will often recognize when on the other side that it would not be fair to hold someone else to that standard. I struggle a lot with how sometimes knowing something is true doesn't always make it feel true, and even though hearing someone else saying it doesn't magically make it all better, I still think it's valuable to hear it from someone else, so if I happen to be right about how you're feeling, nothing about all of this is your fault, and to the extent that you're able to, try not to beat yourself up over your misfortune to get caught in the middle of all this due to circumstances that realistically were outside your control.

title: GitHub - maxilevi/project-hedra at pre-ai · GitHub
content:
Project Hedra
Project Hedra is an ambitious open-world, low-poly RPG. Choose your class, explore endless procedurally generated worlds, unlock different skills and complete procedurally generated quests.
More screenshots at (Screenshots)
Timeline/Context
I started this project when I was in highschool (around 15 yo) in order to learn how OpenGL worked.
The scope creep quickly arrived and after a few years it turned into a fullfledged 3D game and game engine. The codebase has around 100k LOC and the game has first class support for Linux and Windows.
Features
The million lines of code are not in vain. The game and engine are both full of features :)
Game Features
Beatiful procedurally generated worlds
Quests and bosses
100+ items with rarities system
Skills and skill tree system with N+ skills
4 different classes with 2 specializations each ()
Procedurally placed structures generated dynamically
Fishing, crafting, etc
Trading and NPCs
Companions and pets
Beatiful soundtrack
Navigation, maps
Different dimensions
More stuff I don't recall :)
Engine Features
Fully fledged renderer using modern OpenGL
Skinned mesh rendering
Support for loading and playing generic animations
Collada (.dae) parser
Static mesh rendering
Screen space reflections
Screen space ambient occlusion
Bloom, FXAA & MSAA
Modding support
CI for automatically deploying to a Steam beta branch
Localization support
Sound support using OpenAL
Python scripting support
Module system for loading data oriented objects
Steam integration
Fully fledged UI & controls system (dropdowns, buttons, etc.) written from raw OpenGL
Dynamic shader system for reloading during runtime
Frustum culling, occlusion culling,
Mesh simplification for runtime level of detail (LOD)
Skybox support
Shadows
3D trails renderering support
Particle system using object instancing in opengl
bulletphysics integration
Chunk system for infinite worlds support
.ply parsing support
Dynamic meshing support using MarchingCubes
Custom implementation of basic C# primitives and allocators (like Lists) for supporting stack allocated lists and minimizing the automatic runtime allocations (and thus the GC).
1000+ plus test cases
Framework for mocking game components and doing integration testing on games
Image and asset compression for faster loading and smaller size
Entity component system
More stuff I don't recall :)
Interesting bits
WorldRenderer.cs. Renders the entire world in just 3 (actually it depends on how partitioned is the data buffer, but it was designed to be in 3) draw calls (water, terrain, instanced) using glMultiDrawElements.
Block.cs. Core component of the world. Read more at https://maxilevi.com/blog/procedural-meshing-hedra
Fishing.py. Written in Python as a mod script using IronPython, directly interacts with the C# API.
NativeArray.cs Implementation of an array primitive using a custom allocator. The same project provides heap based allocators as well as stac based ones using stackalloc. The idea was to minimize the automatic heap allocations (and thus avoiding the GC) during the game frames.
Interesting facts
The world is fully procedurally generated, there is no world save file. Only the player contents are saved and the world seed. The rest is created at runtime.
The world is voxel based but an isosurface extraction algorithm called Marching Cubes is applied to extract an implicit continous surface from the discrete voxels.
The name "Hedra" comes from tetrahedra which is the shape used in the original iso surface extraction algorithm I implemented Marching Tetrahedra
The game only supports loading .PLY and .DAE models, both which are in plaintext and the models have no textures. Therefore if you put this into perspective, this means I wrote a bunch of text that reads text and creates interactive images from this. I think this is pretty cool.
Screenshots
TODO add more
Code Structure
Overall Architecture
The game is a mod to a base engine. The idea of architecturing this way was to force myself to maintain the mod API up to date, therefore encouraging access to make mods.
Hedra
Basically the entire game. This includes AI logic, components, world generation, module systems, object placement and lots of other stuff.
Hedra.Engine
The core parts of the engine, this defines all the abstractions to the world. It handles rendering, sound, different base systems as well as the general windowing, game loop and platform features. The split was not done at the start so some stuff might still be outside.
Framework
Core primitives used in the engine. This includes heap and stack allocators, custom implementations of lists and arrays as well as wrappers to pointers to native and some other useful primitives
HedraTests
Test suite that
Asset Builder
Command line tool to compress the game assets into convenient binary files. Combines images, models, sound files, shaders into a single binary file with a structure designed for fast data retrieval.
Server
Once upong a time Hedra used to support multiplayer. It worked by doing UDP Hole Punching and having clients communicate P2P, this server was in charge of that. You might also see some networking remnants in the Engine code.
How to build
The build process is pretty straightforward.
Checkout all the submodules
Run the build depedencies scripts
Compile the C# solution
You can check the GitHub actions workflows for some examples on Linux and Windows.

title: Xbox wants you to pay 24 to 40 cents per hour to stream games you already bought - Ars Technica
content:
GAMING BY THE HOUR
Xbox wants you to pay 24 to 40 cents per hour to stream games you already bought
Time-based a la carte charges come on top of the purchase price for the games themselves.
KYLE ORLAND – OCT 21, 2026 10:06 PM | 170
Would you pay a quarter for an hour of access to your Xbox library on the phone? Credit: Microsoft

In September, when Microsoft severely limited the game-streaming buffet available to Game Pass subscribers, the company said non-subscribers would soon be able to “purchase cloud playtime hours through the Xbox Store and stream eligible games they own on supported devices.” Today, Microsoft rolled out those a la carte Cloud Playtime purchases to Xbox Insiders, with prices that might be a bit galling for players who have already purchased these streamable games.
The “introductory launch pricing” for Xbox’s Cloud Playtime purchases is as follows:
10 hours for $4 (~$0.40/hour)
25 hours for $8 (~$0.32/hour)
50 hours for $12 (~$0.24/hour)
Purchased playtime “remains available until it’s used,” Microsoft writes, so you don’t have to worry about your 50-hour purchase expiring before you can use it fully.
Paying for playtime directly like this evokes images of old arcades, where players would invest a quarter or two (in 20th century dollars) often for just a few minutes of gameplay. That kind of metered play has fallen heavily out of fashion, though, in favor of one-time purchases for an all-you-can-play experience at home.
On the surface, paying as low as 24 cents for an hour of streaming game time doesn’t sound completely unreasonable. Remember, though, that these streaming costs come on top of whatever you paid to buy the game in the first place. Unlike an Xbox Game Pass subscription—which includes a few hours of monthly streaming access to hundreds of games as part of the subscription price—these Cloud Playtime packs “require cloud playable game purchase or, for select games, free-to-play access,” Microsoft writes.
Say what you will about the old arcade model, but you didn’t have to buy the cabinet and then pay a quarter per play.
Arcade pricing worked, in part, because you didn’t have to buy the game up front. Not so with a la carte Xbox Cloud Streaming. Credit: Getty Images
ARS VIDEO
How Scientists Respond to Science Deniers
Keep the meter running
Microsoft’s metered Cloud Playtime packs differ from Google’s failed Stadia streaming experiment, which offered unlimited streaming playtime across devices for games you purchased on the platform. Of course, Stadia game purchases also didn’t let you download games for local play on a PC or console, making the overall value proposition quite different. That was especially true after Stadia’s 2022 shutdown made those purchases unplayable (though Google offered full refunds for any and all Stadia purchases at that point).
In 2014, Sony offered a la carte streaming game access for set rental periods as part of its new PlayStation Now service. While that system didn’t require up-front game purchases, the initial pricing was exorbitant, rising to $30 for 90 days of real-time streaming access, even for games that could be purchased outright on disc for less.
Those early streaming price experiments quickly gave way to an all-you-can-stream PlayStation Now subscription plan, which has now morphed into unlimited streaming of select PlayStation games through the top-tier, $20/month (or $160/year) PlayStation Plus Premium plan.
Microsoft is also reminding cloud-curious gamers that Xbox Insiders can test free, ad-supported streams of games they own without buying any playtime packs. That might be the best option for gamers who want to test out a quick Halo session on their phone, rather than maintaining regular streaming access to their Xbox libraries. But Microsoft also says that paid users will get “shorter wait times [and] high-quality streaming,” meaning a deteriorated experience for those who use the ad-supported tier.
In the end, it’s a question of how much of a mass market there is for Xbox Cloud Streaming on its own, rather than as an outgrowth of Xbox Game Pass subscriptions. Last month, Microsoft said that only 4 percent of Game Pass subscribers would be affected by the subscription’s new limits of five to 15 hours of streaming playtime per month.
That suggests only a small minority of Xbox users want to use cloud streaming for a significant portion of their gaming time, even when it was included as a free perk with their existing subscription. How much less interest will there be among non-subscribers who have to pay by the hour for streaming access to games they already own?
KYLE ORLAND SENIOR GAMING EDITOR
Kyle Orland has been the Senior Gaming Editor at Ars Technica since 2012, writing primarily about the business, tech, and culture behind video games. He has journalism and computer science degrees from University of Maryland. He once wrote a whole book about Minesweeper.

title: eMudhra to Exit global SSL/TLS Certificate Business
content:
Will Sharpen Focus on Core Enterprise Solutions and trust services other than SSL/TLS
BENGALURU, INDIA, October 22, 2026 - eMudhra Limited (BSE: 543533 | NSE: EMUDHRA), a global digital trust company, today announced that its Board has decided to voluntarily withdraw from the global SSL/TLS certificate business.
Mr. V. Srinivasan, Chairman, eMudhra Limited referred to the recent incident relating to its global SSL/TLS certificate and indicated that eMudhra handled the recent incident diligently, revoking the affected CAs within 14 hours of discovery and disclosing promptly. There were no end entity certificates issued out of the affected CA’s. Its infrastructure was not compromised and no data was breached. All physical and logical security controls remained intact.
He added that global SSL/TLS is a small part of eMudhra’s business contributing to about 1% of the global revenue. Due to increasing data sovereignty & compliance requirements, complexity and cost associated with this business is increasing over the years. This, paired with the fact that some of the large entities issue the SSL/TLS free of cost, the business potential and RoI of this line of business also has considerably reduced for eMudhra when measured against our cumulative revenue base.
However, the level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business. In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders. For many certifying authorities, SSL/TLS is the whole business. For eMudhra it is one part of a much broader digital solutions portfolio. We will put our energy where we create the most value for customers with Sharpened Focus on Core Enterprise Solutions and trust services other than SSL/TLS.
Seamless transition for customers
Our G1 RSA roots will continue to serve customers until this transition is complete as we work with browser programs and our customers to enable this transition. eMudhra will reach out to affected customers to replace any certificate free of cost from partners through the transition. Revocation and certificate status services will keep running until every issued certificate has expired or been replaced. eMudhra will complete its remaining commitments to the browser root programs, including a full root-cause report.
Core businesses unaffected
eMudhra’s global SSL/TLS infrastructure runs separately from its other operations. The company’s Global digital signature certificate (DSC), eSign, and other signing services, including those in India, its enterprise PKI Solutions (emCA, CertiNext platforms), emSigner eSignature Suite, and its identity and authentication solutions (SecurePass, emAS) are not affected and continue to operate as normal.
About eMudhra
With over 17 years of expertise, eMudhra is a global provider of digital identity, trust, and security solutions, enabling secure digital transformation for banks and financial institutions (BFSI), enterprises, and governments across more than 35 countries worldwide. Its product suite spans CertiNext (PKI and certificate lifecycle management), SecurePass (identity and access management, multi-factor authentication and converged identity), and PrivaTrust (data discovery and consent management for global data-privacy compliance and DSARs), delivering high-assurance digital trust at population scale.

title: Star Map Charts Stars and Constellations of Northern Hemisphere
content:
Mapping the Northern Sky
by Robby Deming
Submitted Map
September 22, 2025 Natural Wonders
Long before satellite navigation and GPS, explorers were already setting their sights toward space. Since we first saw the night sky, humanity has been fascinated by the stars. Over thousands of years, astronomers have tracked the positions of stars and other objects (such as planets, which were described as planetes, or wanderers, by the ancient Greeks). They used the stars to tell stories, make predictions, and even find their way. All of which depended on having an accurate map, mental or otherwise, of the heavens above. 
This stunning map by Florian Winkler catalogs the stars of the night sky in the Northern Hemisphere. It’s built using information from Stellarium, the HYG Database, and W. H. Finlay’s Concise Catalog of Deep-sky Objects.
(Source: Florian Winkler)
The map shows the accurate position and brightness of stars, Messier objects (such as nebulae or spiral galaxies), and constellations. Winkler’s meticulous symbology differentiates stars by their brightness and variability. Labels identify stars and constellations, as well as their Bayer designation.
In the center of the map, you’ll find Polaris, or the North Star. The map’s stereographic projection reflects what you would see if you were to stand at the North Pole and look skyward. Polaris would be directly above you in the center of the sky. The rest of the stars are charted by their celestial coordinates, which function similarly to longitude and latitude. Known as declination and right ascension, the radial grid on the map shows these coordinate lines, reminiscent of meridians and parallels on a terrestrial map. A dashed circle cutting through the center of the map is the ecliptic, which shows the path of the Sun and planets through the sky.
The map charts well-known constellations such as Orion, Ursa Major, and others. (Source: Florian Winkler)
While it’s easy to get lost in the details of the map, it never overwhelms. The map evokes the feeling of gazing at the infinite night sky. Yet it includes enough context to orient yourself and feel like a seasoned astronomer. Winkler’s work blends millennia of celestial knowledge with modern cartographic techniques to create a dazzling map that parallels the wonder of the stars themselves.

title: [2610.27251] AI and The Enclosure of the Scientific Commons
content:
Astrophysics > Instrumentation and Methods for Astrophysics
[Submitted on 19 Oct 2026]
AI and The Enclosure of the Scientific Commons
P. K. G. Williams (Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian)
The scientific literature can be viewed as an "information commons:" an intangible resource that "no one owns and is shared by everyone." There are well-established economic and political frameworks for understanding such commons, emerging from the history of agricultural common lands found in places like preindustrial England. This article provides a primer on the history and these frameworks, and considers a key difference between the information commons and the fields of yore: while information commons are robust and immensely valuable --- some can be said to rank among humanity's greatest achievements --- the English agricultural commons no longer meaningfully exist. The latter are gone not because of the well-known "tragedy of the commons," but rather a phenomenon known as the enclosure movement (~1600--1800) that transformed the common lands into private property. Many observers, then and now, judge enclosure to have been theft at a societal scale. This article argues that artificial intelligence (AI) provides precisely the tools needed to enable a previously-infeasible enclosure of the information commons. Although AI-enabled enclosure does not operate identically to physical enclosure, it shares the key features of turning the commons into private wealth and undermining the social systems that support them (via "slop spam"). The concepts presented in this article can provide a scholarly basis for interrogating the foreboding feeling that AI may represent not just a smash-and-grab, but an attack upon a whole way of life.

title: Uberblok, an interactive museum of ZFS
content:
A museum of ZFS, read in its source
Uberblok
Storage has always had the same enemies: disks that lie, writes cut short, a crash in the middle of an update. ZFS answers them with a handful of ideas. This museum shows them one room at a time, from the code that implements them.
Every animation maps to lines of OpenZFS zfs-2.4.4, frozen at commit 71a9f9578616, and every excerpt links to them. Nothing here is drawn from memory.
Why this museum? ↓
1
2
3
4
Fig. 1. The Hall’s object under the glass: struct uberblock, lines 122–128 of include/sys/uberblock_impl.h at zfs-2.4.4, printed with lines 36–150 of its file.
struct uberblock: the record that names the whole pool
ub_txg: the transaction group of the last sync
ub_rootbp: the block pointer to the root of the tree, the MOS
The listing: lines 36 to 150 of the file, numbered as in the source
The object in the Hall: the uberblock
A pool is millions of blocks spread over several disks. After a crash, the system must find its current, consistent state without scanning any of them. So one small record names the root of everything: the uberblock. It holds a transaction group number, ub_txg, and one block pointer, ub_rootbp; every other block of the pool is reachable from that pointer.
Each disk carries four labels, two at its start and two at its end, and each label keeps a 128 KiB ring of uberblocks. A new uberblock never overwrites the previous one: the uberblock of txg N goes to slot N mod the number of slots (with multihost=on, the last slot is kept for MMP and the ring turns on one slot fewer). On import, ZFS reads every slot of every label and keeps the valid uberblock with the highest txg.
The ring is often said to hold 128 uberblocks. It holds 128 KiB: a slot takes one sector, rounded up to 1 KiB and capped at 8 KiB, so 128 slots on 512-byte sectors, 64 at ashift 11, 32 on the 4K-sector disks of today, 16 beyond. Change the sector size and watch the next txgs take their slots in turn.

newest txg

Every uberblock starts with the same magic number, 0x00bab10c: “oo-ba-bloc”.
Map of the visit
The rooms follow the data: the root and the tree, how the tree changes, where blocks land, what the tree makes possible, then the features built on top, and the engine room, where the museum says how it was made.
00
Hall: the uberblock
The one record that names the whole pool, and the ring that keeps it.
01
History wing
From the first lines of code to OpenZFS, every fact sourced.
02
The tree and the uberblock
Block pointers all the way down, and the write that makes a new tree the current one.
03
Copy-on-write, checksums and self-healing
Why a pool stays consistent without fsck, and how it catches a disk that lies.
04
Transaction groups
Open, quiescing, syncing: how thousands of writes become one commit.
05
The vdevs
Mirror, raidz, draid, log, cache, special: the tree of devices under a pool.
06
RAID-Z
Variable-width stripes, and why there is no write hole.
07
Snapshots and clones
Birth times and deadlists: which snapshot owns this block?
08
The ARC
A cache that learns from what it forgot.
09
Metaslabs and space maps
Finding free space fast, with an append-only log of allocations.
10
ZIL and SLOG
The path of a synchronous write.
11
send / receive
A dataset as a stream, and the increment between two snapshots.
12
Compression, dedup, encryption
Three transforms in the write pipeline, and the honest cost of dedup.
13
Engine room
How this museum was built, and from which commit.
Dedication
Why this museum?
Keeping data safe is critical work, and seldom seen. A file system is handed everything people keep, and it has to stay right through crashes, failing disks and writes cut short. One of the principles ZFS was designed on, in Bill Moore’s words: never, ever trust the underlying hardware.1
This museum pays homage to that piece of engineering, and to the people who built it. Jeff Bonwick led the development of ZFS, with Bill Moore as co-lead;1 Matt Ahrens was one of its two original authors.2 The work began in 2001 with two engineers at Sun Microsystems3 and was integrated into Solaris on 31 October 2005,4 a step Bonwick summed up as 584 files, 92,000 lines of change, 56 patents, 5 years.4 On 17 November he wrote: I’m incredibly proud of the ZFS team, and deeply grateful: no one person can do something on this scale.5
It pays homage, too, to the engineering at Sun in those years, where engineers published how their systems worked: the slab allocator, presented by Jeff Bonwick at USENIX in 1994;6 DTrace, by Bryan Cantrill, Michael Shapiro and Adam Leventhal, in 2004;7 and the source of ZFS itself, released under the CDDL as part of OpenSolaris.3
And to those who carry it on: OpenZFS, announced in 20132 and founded by members of the Linux, FreeBSD, Mac OS X and illumos communities.2 The release this museum reads lists more than 700 people in its AUTHORS file.

content:
Dungeon Generation in the Gnomish Mines of NetHack
2026-10-18 | Boris
Ok, this one is really best explained with a visualiser:
NetHack’s level generation has a lot of interesting things, but I wanted to focus on the Gnomish Mines because of their use of Cellular Automata. This gives it an organic caves feel, while the majority of the game is spent in square rooms.
It’s very straightforward:
Randomly pick 40% of the cells to be floor
Apply four passes of Cellular Automata
Fix up disconnected caves with extra corridors
Let’s dive into the cellular automata specifically. There’s only two states – floor or rock. And each pass works by counting how many floor tiles are in the 8-neighbor hood of each cell.
Pass 1: 0-2 → rock; 3-4 → unchanged, 5-8 → floor
Pass 2: 0-4 → unchanged; 5 → rock; 6-8 → unchanged
Pass 3: 0-2 → rock; 3-8 → unchanged.
Pass 4: same as pass 3
Interestingly, pass 1 is unbuffered. Each cell is updated in place before moving to the next cell. All the rest are buffered – all cells have new computed values, then the entire grid updated at once.
Pass 1 creates floors near other floors, and creates rocks near other rocks. I’d call this a “clustering” pass, that pushes the random tiles towards wide open areas of tiles. The unbuffering is important here so that you don’t flop-flop, turning something rock→floor near something turning floor→rock.
Passes 3 and 4 are erosion routines, it’s a very common use of cellular automata. If you have 6-8 rocks nearby, then you also become a rock. That tends to smooth out corners, and delete tiny islands.
Pass 2 though… It turns cells to rock if they have exactly 5 floor neighbors (i.e. 3 rock neighbors). I’m still struggling to understand what purpose this is intended to achieve. Any ideas?

How to Design Flowers — Nick Desnoyer
A plant biologist in England is using genetic engineering, breeding, and pathogens to design and create flowers that exist nowhere else on Earth.
ASIMOV PRESS AND NIKO MCCARTY
OCT 08, 2026
23
3
4
Share
Transcript
Nick Desnoyer, a plant biologist in Norwich, England, is designing and creating flowers that don’t exist anywhere in nature. In today’s episode, he reveals his next project: Paintunia, a petunia that acts as a living canvas.
Nick has engineered these petunias to include an inducible gene. When he lightly touches their buds with a clear molecule called dexamethasone, the molecules seep into cells, switch on the gene, and cause them to make a pigment. The result is a paintable flower, where molecules literally control which colors show up in particular places. Nick’s plan is ultimately to engineer these petunias to express three separate inducible genes, or biosynthetic pathways, for cyan, magenta, and yellow. For a prior project, Nick turned Arabidopsis, a small (and quite ugly) plant that researchers commonly use in research, into little pink “micro-roses.”
We filmed this episode surrounded by flowers. Nick patiently explained to me how each one gets its shape and pigmentation; how he combines breeding and genetic engineering to make new flowers; and how he searches scientific papers for mutations to figure out which plant crosses to make next. His ultimate dream is to build a botanical garden full of weird and wonderful flowers that exist nowhere else.
